The growth in natural language processing is largely uncontrolled, driven by a widespread reliance on text-based data that is often poorly quality-controlled. This leads to a multitude of serious incidents, ranging from the spread of misinformation to cases of physical harm, that methodically go unreported. As a result, the benefits of NLP technologies come at a significant cost for society. Instead of rectifying these flaws in the current, chaotic system, we propose a more structured approach where incidents are documented and analyzed. The AI Incident Repository, a comprehensive database of NLP system failures, is presented here. It serves as a resource for identifying recurring issues, promoting reflection on system limitations, and informing discussions on ethical implications. The repository's benefits and potential challenges are discussed, along with a proposed framework for creating and maintaining the repository. Additionally, a preliminary evaluation of the Incident Repository's effectiveness is presented using news articles and human evaluation methods. This preliminary findings demonstrate that having a centralized repository of incidents can raise researchers' awareness of potential errors in their own work. Based on these observations, several possible future applications of the Incident Repository are envisioned. It is hoped that this repository will contribute to an ongoing discussion on mitigating the negative consequences of NLP and ultimately lead to a more responsible development of these technologies. In particular, it is intended to aid researchers and developers in identifying and addressing recurring errors, promoting reflection on system limitations, informing discussions on ethical implications, and fostering a culture of safety and accountability within the NLP community. A new order relationship, the binomial depth, has been developed for models that use success/failure probabilities to rank observations, allowing the creation of depth-based quantiles similar to those from classical parametric methods. The binomial depth applies a transformation to the data in the form of a probability distribution, creating a new representation of the order relationship. The resulting quantiles are determined by analyzing this transformed representation. Our approach focuses on the binomial distribution but the method can be adapted to other probability distributions as well. The Theophillus-Arnaud and Tukey orders are special cases of the binomial depth. A key challenge is estimating depth-based quantiles without assuming a specific distribution, so a new method based on depth-weighted local polynomial estimation is proposed to provide finite-sample confidence intervals for the quantiles. The method is developed further by applying a transformation inverse to the Isometric Log-Change function, enabling the use of classical parametric methods to estimate binomial depth quantiles. Our approach is demonstrated with simulations and applications to real data, including analysis of election outcomes and measurement of door width. The proposed method is available in the R package BinDepth. Keywords: binomial depth, isometric log-change, deep learning, quantile estimation.

Recent findings suggest that the number of detected exoplanets below this break point may have been underestimated in earlier studies. To further investigate this issue, we re-examined the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample from 2014, which consisted of 363 exoplanets that had been discovered using this technique. Our analysis focused on the 138 sub-Saturn mass exoplanets that had been detected and found that the detection rate for these exoplanets was not significantly lower than expected based on a theoretical model. Our approach provides a clear distinction between genuine global aggregation phenomena and other methods that may produce similar outcomes. Building on this framework, we develop a rigorous formulation for global aggregation dynamics in a general context. This formulation enables us to identify the underlying transport equation, which the governing particle dynamics is shown to be in precise alignment with. Consequently, we are able to derive a universal criterion for achieving exact microscopic closed solutions. Moreover, we apply our framework to achieve this goal for two specific models: Fermi-Pasta-Ulam and Goodling's equation, thus obtaining precise solutions that were previously unknown. Additionally, we establish micro-macro equivalences for both of these models. In the case of Fermi-Pasta-Ulam, we successfully generalize a prior study by Markert, Pllaha, and Stark, while our work on Goodling's equation is an original contribution. Furthermore, we numerically verify that the proposed micro-macro mapping for Fermi-Pasta-Ulam produces accurate results when compared to high-resolution simulations. Our study aims to revive and expand transport theory, and we believe that our framework will be adaptable to a wide range of other particle system models as well. In the course of our work, we also identify an important general challenge that we hope will be addressed by future research: developing a suitable notion of 'transport solution.' This challenge is particularly relevant to our examination of the long-term asymptotics of solutions derived from initial data that are relatively close to equilibrium. To achieve this, we utilize data from the CANDELS project, combining information from the Hubble Space Telescope with modeling of galaxy ultraviolet spectra from the Keck Observatory. As a result, we are able to accurately model the distribution of stars within a radius of approximately 3.5 optical points in a sample of 1017 galaxies from the Hubble Goodrich catalog. To assess the alignment of the major axis of galaxies, we compare it to the direction of radio emission in radio-loud AGN and the axis of light polarization in type 1 and type 2 AGN, finding significant variations depending on the AGN sub-class. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between galaxy structure and other characteristics, such as the color and morphology of the galaxy, its stellar mass, and the presence of a central bulge, as well as how these relationships are influenced by the AGN. Our research also highlights previously unrecognized similarities and differences between various types of AGN, with implications for understanding their existence and development. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification or unsupervised depth assessment to
achieve this. While classification methods have been extensively studied, very few
have examined the efficacy of depth assessment in this context. In our research,
we evaluate various depth assessment methods for pre-training semantic segmentation
models, proposing a novel benchmark called DepthAssessment-semantic to fill
this gap. Our results indicate that unsupervised depth assessment outperforms
classification-based pre-training on all the tested datasets we utilized. Moreover,
our experiments reveal that xDEEP, an advanced deep learning model, excels in
pre-training semantic segmentation models compared to other state-of-the-art
methods like ResNet-50 and DualPathNet. Additionally, to improve the speed and
efficiency of semantic segmentation models, we suggest reducing the pre-trained
model's parameter count using the parameter reduction method. Our investigation
shows that employing these reduced models leads to significant performance gains
while still achieving superior results compared to classification-based
pre-training. Hence, DepthAssessment-semantic can serve as a valuable resource
for researchers seeking to leverage unsupervised depth assessment for efficient
semantic segmentation model pre-training. The code and model weights are publicly
available at https://github.com/yhenonard/DepthAssessment-semantic.

The ability to generate compelling stories from continuous data is highly desirable in fields like education, finance, and sports analysis. Despite the presence of several neural story generation methods, they often rely on specific story structures or domains like conversation, which limits their applicability to other fields. To overcome these limitations, we present a novel story generation method called TCube that uses a universal neural architecture to generate stories in various domains. Our approach combines a hierarchical topic model to mimic a neural story generator's internal structure and leverages a neural reader to assess the coherence of generated stories. To further improve story coherence, we propose a novel strategy involving the sequential merging of topics. Evaluations on both the Conversational AI and TimeSeries datasets reveal that TCube surpasses state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin in multiple metrics, including story coherence and overall score. Moreover, we demonstrate through human evaluations that TCube accurately learns a unified story structure that outperforms previously proposed structures. To facilitate future research, we provide an implementation of TCube on GitHub. Additionally, we created and made available a new dataset called ConversationalAI that features 41,693 stories in various domains, which can be accessed through this link. Our dataset offers an exclusive collection of stories that can be used as training data for story generation models. Furthermore, we invite researchers to participate in a story generation challenge by following these instructions. We are excited to collaborate with the research community on this project! I would also like to express my gratitude to P. Barber, S. Chen, and S. Yang for their exceptional research assistance. The ATLAS experiment has provided the LHC with precise measurements of beauty meson decays that involve CP violation, electroweak interactions, or unusual nuclear processes. CP violation in beauty mesons serves as a crucial test of the Standard Model and potential pathways to new physics. Uncommon decays of these mesons can yield insights into production mechanisms and fragmentation processes. This study reviews recent ATLAS findings in multiple categories, including (i) beauty meson decays that exhibit CP violation, (ii) electroweak interactions such as $W+b$ and $W+c$ jets, and (iii) unusual processes like $\J/\psi$, $\psi2S$, and $\Upsilon$ decays into final states containing di-leptons or light hadrons. Furthermore, the study discusses ongoing and planned research in this area, focusing on potential future advancements with increased luminosity and improved detector components. With enhanced sensitivity, the ATLAS experiment is expected to deliver more precise measurements in this field, thereby significantly expanding our understanding of beauty meson physics. For example, the experiment may be able to re-evaluate $W+b$ jets or explore rare $\Upsilon$ decays such as $\Upsilon \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ in the near future. These potential breakthroughs will be crucial for optimizing the ATLAS detection capabilities in preparation for high-luminosity running at the LHC. By doing so, the experiment will be well-positioned to deliver the LHC's maximum scientific potential, thereby significantly advancing our understanding of particle physics. This could even involve detecting long-overdue processes such as $\Upsilon \rightarrow \gamma\gamma$. These efforts reflect the ongoing efforts of the ATLAS collaboration to optimize its analysis tools and strategies in preparation for future high-luminosity running at the LHC. Our study addresses the galaxy diversity problem in deep learning, focusing on
classifying various galaxy types. To evaluate essential factors for model performance,
we conducted comprehensive analyses on the Deep Learning Benchmark (DLB) platform
with multiple benchmark datasets. Our experiments examined key variables including
dataset size, network complexity, and training data distribution. We also analyzed
the impact of using pre-trained weights and the effectiveness of using early stopping.
Our findings highlight specific variables - network complexity and training data distribution
- that significantly influence model performance. They outperform other considered
factors, such as dataset size, for distinguishing between galaxy types. Based on our
research, we suggest that adjusting the training data distribution is a more effective
approach than refining network structure to enhance galaxy classification performance. 
Our study also demonstrates the suitability of the DLB platform for benchmarking
deep learning tasks across various domains. Our findings are expected to contribute to
developing more effective methods for the galaxy diversity problem. The code for this
project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Deep-Learning-Benchmark/galaxy.git.

To address these issues, we introduce Pando, a novel volunteer computing system designed for individual usage through web browsers. Pando's key innovations include its custom-built JavaScript sauce, separate frontend and backend components, and simultaneous support of Docker and Kubernetes. Additionally, Pando offers several efficient management mechanisms to optimize resource allocation and task distribution. Our comprehensive evaluations of Pando are conclusive: it surpasses existing platforms in its ability to recruit individual users, while also achieving faster computation speeds and greater application scalability. Notably, Pando demonstrates impressive scalability by deploying on Google's Cloud Platform, showcasing its potential to assist various scientific research fields with its enhanced features and infrastructure. To further facilitate community adoption, the full source code of Pando is now freely accessible at github.com/parad/pando. Additionally, more information about the research can be found at parad-lab.org/pando. We proudly invite volunteers to join the Pando community and utilize this powerful computing platform for their research needs. Currently, users can participate in the development of Pando by translating its website into different languages, which is a valuable contribution to the project. In the future, we will regularly post job postings on our website to recruit programmers, researchers, and other professionals to assist with various research initiatives. In recent times, the concept of Hardware-as-a-Service has gained significant traction, however, it poses significant security risks due to shared hardware. Several research initiatives have focused on mitigating these security threats through the utilization of secure, dedicated environments within the hardware. Despite these efforts, the existing solutions still fall short in addressing key security concerns, primarily due to the fact that the protected environments often lack critical system services required to execute complex system functions. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework called Flatee that enables the seamless interoperability of secure environments by allowing them to collaborate with each other. This framework achieves collaboration through the use of remote access to shared resources, protected by sophisticated security mechanisms that prevents the sharing of sensitive data. Furthermore, we model and evaluate the security capabilities of conventional training methods, and propose an innovative solution called Federated Learning inside Enclaves. Our experimental results demonstrate that Flatee can facilitate secure, distributed neural network training across multiple secure environments with minimal performance overhead. Notably, the overhead is so minimal that it is comparable to executing the same training locally within a single secure environment. This outstanding performance is made possible by the use of reliable network connections and the efficient design of the HLIE training method. In particular, our experiments have shown that using HLIE we can achieve a linear scaling of the training process up to 128 participants, and the use of a robust classification model does not hinder the performance even when there are multiple participants involved. This is in stark contrast to the existing solutions, where the use of classification models often leads to performance degradation and diminished scalability. In conclusion, Flatee offers a revolutionary new approach to collaborative machine learning security, and it has the potential to transform the development of secure, distributed neural networks. This approach is innovative because it enables the scalable distribution of neural network training across multiple secure environments without compromising performance. This groundbreaking work has numerous practical applications and could potentially lead to new developments in the field of secure, distributed machine learning. The source code of Flatee is publicly available on GitHub. We anticipate that our research will the foundation for numerous future research initiatives in this domain. The ability to program various phases ahead of time is a key feature that makes electromagnetically responsive materials so appealing for use in the transmission electron microscope (TEM). If a material with this capability can be introduced into the TEM and converge the electron beam in a controlled manner, it could potentially be used to correct the microscope's lenses. Loihi, designed by Intel, utilizes a neuromorphic architecture that combines spike-based computation with temporal integration. We developed an alternative implementation of Loihi's processor unit and surrounding circuit mechanics within the context of the Brian network simulator. Under benchmarking, our findings indicate that the Loihi emulator exhibits comparable performance to the original Loihi hardware, specifically with respect to memory usage and operation speed. We discovered that the primary factors influencing emulator performance are temporal integration duration and spike propagation distance. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the Brian network simulator 2 is an suitable platform for systems engineering and neuroscience research applications due to its ability to efficiently emulate complex neural circuits. We anticipate that our Loihi emulator will contribute to advancements in Loihi hardware development, systems engineering, and the understanding of underlying brain processes. We also expect it to aid in Loihi's future integration into large-scale neural networks, well-tuned for energy-efficient spike-based computation. You can access the Loihi emulator through the brain2lohi package on GitHub and PyPI, as well as view relevant documentation at the loihi-brian.org website. These storms exhibit substantial electron enhancement, leading to intense radio emission across various frequencies. To better comprehend the complex behavior of these storms, it's crucial to study the relationships between related quantities during minor flares, which cause constrictions in the storm source area, resulting in sound-wave generation and associated radio emission at metric wavelengths. By investigating such flares, which often go undetected in X-ray and hard UV bands, it's possible to gain valuable insights into the role of current-free magnetic field reconfiguration. This research involves a solar active region studied on June 6, 2020, where noise storm sources with clear source motion displayed rapid changes in their radio emission pattern, electron density, and the associated sound-wave amplitude. These sources experienced rapid motion accompanied by significant changes in their characteristics, indicating a linked evolutionary process likely initiated by a microflare detected using X-ray data from SDO. During this event, the isolated active region sub-element experienced an X-ray brightness temperature increase, suggesting the involvement of magnetic field twist or tilting in the noise storm source area, which is consistent with the behavior of solar jets. This study confirms that noise storm sources are complex and dynamic, involving the interaction and contraction of magnetic field flux tubes, as well as the acceleration and beam propagation of electrons, charging the solar atmosphere and generating metric-wavelength radio emission. Moreover, noise storm sources may provide an alternative indicator of minor flares and the associated magnetic field changes that are currently not being adequately monitored. By closely observing these sources and their behavior, it's possible to gain further insights into the dynamic nature of the solar upper atmosphere and the mechanisms driving noise storm formation. This, in turn, may enhance our understanding of solar jitters and their role in the solar atmosphere. The spherically symmetric merging of a dust cloud with a black hole is modeled, where the cloud's formation is confined to a specific radius due to conservation of angular momentum. Assuming a Steady-State Transonic solution, where the fluid's speed and pressure are constant, we derive a radial equation for the fluid's trajectory under the influence of gravity and angular momentum, and find that the fluid will settle at a specific radius, known as the Accretion Radius, where the fluid's speed equals the Eddington speed. When a Steady-State Transonic flow is achieved, the Accretion Radius is determined to be $2.84$ times the gravitational radius, and powered by a black hole with an initial mass of $10^8 \odot$, this Accretion Radius would be approximately $5.82 \times 10^{15}$ meters or $58,200$ times the radius of the Sun. Additionally, a relationship for the Accretion Radius in relation to Spin and Mass of the black hole is established, and simulation results for various black holes are plotted and tabulated, with an illustration of these results provided in Figure 1 in the main article. Furthermore, a model of a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way is used, where it is calculated that the Accretion Radius would be approximately $2.67$ times the gravitational radius, or approximately $2.05 \times 10^{17}$ meters, roughly equivalent to thirty-five times the radius of the Sun. These results imply that a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way could be significantly lighter than generally estimated if it were feeding on nearby star-forming regions. Finally, a theoretical model for the luminosity of an accreting black hole, based on the Accretion Radius and angular momentum of the fluid, is proposed and used to calculate the luminosity of several black holes, with tabulated results and an illustration in Figure 2 in the main article. This model reveals that an accreting black hole could be much less luminous than a non-accreting black hole of the same mass, and that a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way could be much less luminous than generally estimated if it were feeding on nearby star-forming regions. The dynamic interaction between matter and radiation is a fundamental concept that underlies a broad range of phenomena, from the emission spectra of Raman scattered light to the electromagnetic signals given off by rapidly moving atoms. Researchers in the field of table-top gravitational wave detection have proposed using slotted mirrors as slotted michelson interferometers to detect the gravitational effect of freely falling objects. From an atomic perspective, this setup forms a resonant system that can cause electromagnetic emission when atoms move through it. Our study focuses on this interface from the atom's point of view, using the quantum ray model to investigate the electromagnetic emission produced by atoms moving toward or away from a slender mirror, as well as the radiation emitted when they recoil against or accelerate past it. The results show that the electromagnetic signals given off by the atoms are in the form of dipoles or higher-order poles, depending on the atomic motion, and that the energy levels of these signals are influenced by the atomic velocity and acceleration. Our findings could be observed using tabletop equipment, and we suggest that observing this emission using atoms like rubidium or yttrium may provide a direct visual representation of the gravitational effect experienced by these atoms as they move through the slotted michelson interferometer. This could serve as conclusive evidence of the electromagnetic emission produced by rapidly moving atoms, and it may also provide a way to measure the gravitational field produced by an object that is falling or moving horizontally. In particular, our results indicate that the electromagnetic emission produced by the atom is most clearly visible when it is moving through the center of the slotted michelson interferometer and when the atomic velocity is very low. In such cases, the electromagnetic signal given off by the atom takes the form of two distinct pulses that are separated by the time it takes for the atom to travel through the slotted michelson interferometer, and the energy levels of these pulses are influenced by the atomic acceleration. Similarly, when the atom is moving through the slotted michelson interferometer and experiences a change in velocity, the electromagnetic emission produced by the atom takes the form of two distinct pulses that are influenced by the atomic acceleration. Our study indicates that the energy levels of these pulses are dependent on the atomic acceleration, and they may provide a way to measure the acceleration experienced by the atom as it moves through the slotted michelson interferometer. At the center of this area, a massive star cluster has been found, which we are studying now. Our latest findings involve a massive star that has been identified as one of the largest of its kind in the region. Handwritten documents, crucial for research in Natural Language Processing and possible future applications in Deep Learning, are severely hindered by poor image quality due to factors like aging, handwritten style, and distortion. To rectify this issue, a framework is developed to enhance degraded document images, featuring an end-to-end adversarial network architecture that integrates reading and improvement tasks. The framework comprises a text reader task to derive meaningful information from degraded images and a text generator task to produce synthetic text for reference, while an generator and discriminator duo works to generate and distinguish high-quality from real degraded document images. The integration of reading and improvement tasks and the adversarial network architecture are key components of success. Performance is evaluated through the evaluation of generated text and the Bitrate penalty metrics on datasets NII-Handwitning-300K and NII-Handwriting-400K. The proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to traditional restoration methods and a Text Reader based approach, demonstrating state-of-the-art results on datasets NII-Handwriting-300K and NII-Handwriting-400K. The framework is made accessible via an open-source platform for research purposes. Source: arxiv.org/abs/2202.06775

The extraction of ID card information has become a fundamental component of various applications in Indonesia. Previously, this process relied heavily on manual input, but recent advancements in Optical Character Recognition technology have made it possible to automate this task. Our research builds upon existing knowledge of ID card extraction, incorporating Indonesian-specific font styles while leveraging the power of Regular Expressions and deep Learning-based OCR integration. Furthermore, we have made our ID card extractor framework, which integrates OCR and NLP, available as open-source software for the benefit of the community. Additionally, we have created an NLP-based model to enhance the accuracy of extracts, particularly for the "temporary address" field, using techniques such as BERT. Our research achieves state-of-the-art results, achieving a 94% success rate for the "temporary address" field. Our extracted data fields have been accredited by the Indonesian authorities as officially recognized data sets. Our Indonesian ID extractor has been successfully implemented in various real-world applications, processing a significant volume of data and demonstrating its effectiveness through an analysis of its accuracy. Our research presents an in-depth comparison with existing similar solutions, highlighting the uniqueness of our extractor in terms of its use of NLP for error correction and its integration of OCR for ID card image analysis. Our findings indicate that our extractor outperforms existing solutions in terms of accuracy, convenience, and scalability. Our research also addresses common error patterns in ID card extraction, specifically those related to the "temporary address" field, and presents two distinct types of errors, which can be resolved respectively by an NLP-based model and by manually reviewing the ID card image. Our findings are then validated through an experiment involving 50,000 ID card images, demonstrating the efficacy of our extractor in correcting errors in this data set. Our research showcases the versatility of our ID extractor, illustrating how it can be adapted to extract information from various types of documents, not just ID cards, through an example of extracting information from receipts, utilizing OCR and NLP. Our research achieves a 85% success rate in extracting information from receipts, showcasing its ease of use and convenience. Our research concludes by highlighting the accomplishments of our research and the benefits it has brought, specifically in terms of demonstrating the accuracy of NLP-powered ID card extraction and promoting its use as a standard method, in addition to making available an open-source software for the community. Data-intensive applications in intelligent transportation systems (ITS) rely heavily on the reliability of IEEE 802.11p wireless communication systems. Nevertheless, they are susceptible to signal degradation stemming from interference, vehicles, and other forms of channel fluctuations. The IEEE 802.11p systems utilize 5.9 GHz short-range radar technology and rely on the channel state information (CSI) provided by their receivers. Consequently, developing and deploying high-performance IEEE 802.11p receivers capable of providing accurate CSI is of significant importance. This paper proposes an innovative, long short-term memory (LSTM)-driven 802.11p receiver architecture designed to overcome signal weakness and diverse channel conditions by leveraging deep packet modeling. The proposed method's performance and practical applicability were evaluated through simulations conducted on various 802.11p test beds, including vehicles, urban traffic scenarios, and urban city environments, as well as an indoor parking lot setting. The results show that the proposed LSTM-driven approach outperforms other comparative methods and achieves improved accuracy and reliability in diverse environments. Additionally, the code for the proposed architecture has been openly contributed on the GitHub platform under the name "LSTMPM_802.11p". This effort aims to support and facilitate the development of 802.11p receivers by providing a high-degree of design flexibility and enabling easy integration of the proposed LSTM-driven receiver into existing 802.11p systems. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be generalized and applied to other wireless communication systems with similar technical characteristics. The ultimate goal is to enhance the reliability of ITS services through a robust and reliable wireless communication infrastructure. The work presented in this paper marks a significant step towards achieving this objective. The source code for the simulations is available at https://github.com/AmrAbouelkereem/LSTMPM_802.11p. Digital image enhancement plays a crucial role in various scientific applications, particularly in space research, where image restoration techniques are essential for obtaining precise information about celestial objects and their environments. The lack of high-quality data in this field necessitates the development of efficient image enhancement methods. In response, we introduce a novel approach, called Celestial Image Tinting, which utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks to improve the quality of celestial images. The proposed method comprises two main stages: primary enhancement and detailed correction. The former aims to enhance the overall image quality, while the later focuses on refining details through a task-specific loss function. To further optimize the model, we also explored the effect of varying network depths and data augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Furthermore, we conducted an user study to verify the quality of the generated images. The code for our method is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ESO-Pegase/CITNet GitHub. The Pegase website also offers access to our pre-trained model and demonstration: https://esopegase.fr/CITNet. The starfish dataset used in our experiments can be downloaded from: https://www.zooniverse.org/tasks/stars_fish/. The contribution of this work can be summarized into three key areas: (i) image enhancement, (ii) Celestial Image Tinting, and (iii) public outreach. The latter involved collaborating with Zooniverse and ESO-Pegase to integrate our model into the starfish task, which enabled us to gather over 180,000 annotations from multiple classes of users. As a result, we were able to gain valuable insights from annotated data and demonstrate the feasibility of Celestial Image Tinting. Moreover, we were able to verify the effectiveness of our model through an user study. The combination of deep learning and crowd annotating has led to the creation of an extensive dataset, which will be made available at: https://esopegase.fr/CIDataset. The proposed method is likely to have far-reaching applications in space research and other fields, and its source code will be publicly available on GitHub. Ultimately, we aim to develop image enhancement techniques that are grounded in physical models and guided by the input of human experts. The challenge of deep learning in space research involves translating images into physical models and incorporating the knowledge of human experts into this process. The universal approximation theorem confirms that feedforward neural networks with one hidden layer can accurately model any continuous function. However, the underlying learning process remains unclear, as we experimentally observed overextended training times despite convergence. Inspired by the theorem's proof, we developed a novel learning algorithm free from gradients, based on the theorem's principles, which demonstrates the following: (i) each iteration is a full learning cycle, unaffected by the network's previous states; (ii) the learning process is autonomous and self-contained. This learning algorithm is now seamlessly integrated into a neural network structure, which we call Universal Approximation Neural Networks (UANN), and the entire code is made publicly available on GitHub. Additionally, the UANN model has been successfully applied to solve complex regression and classification problems. The experimental results show significant reductions in training time and outperformed performance on various problem datasets. The integration of the universal approximation theorem's insights into the UANN learning algorithm has enabled us to create a more efficient neural network structure. The experimental findings indicate that the UANN model produces better results and reduces the training time compared to other methods. Furthermore, the gradient-free learning algorithm enabled us to observe novel phenomena during the learning process, such as the emergence of local minima and the reorganization of hidden neurons, which can be beneficial for understanding neural networks and using them in other research areas. As communication requirements continue to evolve, innovative technologies like metamaterials and metasurfaces are redefining the boundaries of light manipulation. Recent breakthroughs in flat optics have facilitated the development of compact, high-performance optical systems, and new configurations of metasurfaces that combine multiple functions are now being introduced. We have conceptually designed and theoretically studied a unique dual metastructure capable of guiding line waves, which could be applied in two-dimensional optical systems. By utilizing coordinate transformation design, we created a non-Abelian dual metastructure that can replicate the functionality of a Monge matrix and thus efficiently guide line waves. The proposed structure consists of an array of symmetric rectangular plates with side plates oriented at 45-degree angles, and our calculations show that it can generate line waves with diverse properties by adjusting the plate spacing and arrangement. The anticipated applications of this design include high-performance flat optics, radiators, and sensors. The study has provided a fundamental analysis of the designed metastructure and offered practical suggestions for implementation. Furthermore, we have explored the general applicability of our design to other types of line waves. Cognitive AI algorithms inspired by brain function are now widely used to create intelligent systems capable of learning. However, these algorithms struggle to adapt to large-scale and resource-constrained environments. To address this challenge, our research focuses on developing a novel, architecture-independent approach that enables large-scale multi-agent cooperative learning within complex systems. We introduce a dynamic and adaptable data storage solution that extracts and processes sensory data from ongoing interactions between human and robotic teammates. To facilitate transparent and explainable decision-making, our approach employs a unified graph data structure to integrate knowledge from various AI algorithms and accurately replicate their behavior. Furthermore, a distributed data storage system enables scalable transmission of learned information across team members. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present two experiments involving intricate robotic scenarios that demonstrate our ability to learn and implement effective team strategies through observation, as well as transfer learning across distinct tasks. We openly provide the source code and demonstration videos on the m3c website for the community to reproduce our results. We believe that our research will contribute to the development of scalable cognitive AI algorithms capable of learning in large-scale multi-agent environments. In the future, we plan to further refine our approach by incorporating more AI algorithms and demonstrating human learning within these environments. We envision that our work, fueled by the desire to create transparent and scalable multi-agent learning frameworks, will aid in building more efficient and dynamic teams of human and robotic collaborators. This result has been confirmed through simulations, showing that the bias-corrected estimator performs at least as well as traditional methods in estimating the average absolute deviation. Moreover, this estimator is shown to be consistent under certain conditions. A simulation study reveals that our proposed bias-corrected estimator achieves greater efficiency while maintaining at least the same level of bias correction as compared to alternative estimators. It is worth noting that the bias-correction properties of our proposed estimator apply when the data are drawn independently, but extensions for dependent data are also provided. Link prediction in knowledge graphs has been effectively employed to uncover hidden connections between entities in unlabelled data. This paper investigates another application of this technique - relation discovery, which involves identifying kernel entities with specific characteristics that are not explicitly marked in the data. By treating realted entities as nodes in an graph, we can train a model to predict the characteristics of these entities. Our proposed method, which uses knowledge graph connection prediction to enhance relation discovery, involves constructing a graph with entities and their characteristics, then using a model to predict the relationships between these entities. This predicted relationship matrix is then integrated with a relation discovery model to prioritize real and relevant characteristics. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, our method shows significant improvements in datasets with complex relationships and limited annotated data. Further analysis highlights the effectiveness of our method in identifying entity characteristics. Code implementation is available on the GitHub repository. By introducing modulated modulated cyclic activation modules (m^2CAN modules) as building blocks of mCANT-II, we overcome the limitations of traditional local feature extraction methods which struggle to handle data with intricate long-range relationships and challenging spatial arrangements. Additionally, we find that the mCANT-II generates more readable feature maps with the m^2CAN module acting as a spatial attention mechanism to isolate specific regions of interest. Furthermore, we successfully apply the mCANT-II to vehicle semantic segmentation, taking into account the unique characteristics of vehicle images, and achieve superior performance compared to competing approaches. Our method draws on concepts from semi-supervised learning, employing cause and influence attributes to tackle this challenge. The 'cause' attribute refers to domains with established statistical connections, while the 'influence' attribute relies on empirical findings from relevant studies. Our semi-generative model learns from paired cause-influence samples, incorporating domain-specific features to adapt to shifting covariates. This paper introduces a novel concept of "chief depth" for elements in R, which is based on a specific non-normal form known as the chief form. It also establishes a relationship between the chief depth and another depth invariant called the lattice depth. By optimizing the chief form algorithm, the paper presents a dynamic method to compute chief forms and demonstrates that chief forms exist for elements in R that have a finite chief depth but do not exist for those with an infinite chief depth. A key finding shows that an element has a finite chief depth if and only if its lattice depth is finite. To prove these results, the paper introduces a concept of "flag independence" for finite point sets and demonstrates that an element has a finite chief depth when, and only when, its lattice depth is finite and its point set contains at least two flag-independent pairs. This proves an extension of a theorem by Hurder and Sather-Wagstaff. The Hubbard model, a fundamental representation of quantum electronics, faces a significant obstacle known as the sign problem. This limitation restricts the use of certain numerical reconstruction methods like the Monte Carlo method at finite temperatures. Researchers have devised various techniques to overcome the sign problem, such as the Taylor series expansion or the Taylor series expansion with analytic continuation. A relatively underexplored approach involves the application of neural networks to predict the complex rotation required for sign correction. Our study shows that using complex-valued neural networks for this purpose yields more accurate results than their real-valued counterparts. Moreover, we discovered that using Taylor series expansions beyond the third order does not significantly improve the accuracy. A new type of particle, the flavon, is proposed as a field that couples to the Higgs field while being a complex representation of the Littlest Higgs Orbitsim group. Theoretical models are developed to create a mechanism that spontaneously breaks flavon symmetry in two ways: either by generating a mass for the flavon or by combining it with a scalar field into a singlet. These models are evaluated for their stability in three scenarios where the flavon is related to $SU(2)/U(1)$ symmetry breaking, resulting in different mass and interaction properties for the flavon in each scenario. High-stakes data analysis demands unwavering reliability, especially in critical decision-making scenarios. Deterministic methods may offer absolute certainty, yet they can be compromised by sophisticated adversaries. On the other hand, probabilistic methods like Bayesian estimation are more adaptable and commonly used. However, traditional Bayesian estimators often neglect the possibility of manipulative interference, which can be catastrophic. This paper introduces a groundbreaking framework that not only accounts for the risk of interference but also guarantees a degree of resilience through stringent testing. This framework is based on building a "safety net" around the estimated parameter, ensuring that any actual value within this net is more likely than its perfect counterpart. By developing Bayesian estimators that meet this safety net criterion, we can maintain the admissibility and consistency of these estimators. Moreover, we illustrate the practical application of this framework in estimating the parameters of a linear model under hostile conditions, utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods that require only minor modifications to existing algorithms. Our framework presents a versatile approach to ensuring the reliability of statistical analysis in the face of adversity. This research is the first to incorporate robustness as a priority in the design of Bayesian estimators, making it an essential framework for any high-stakes analysis. Additionally, we demonstrate that our estimators excel in various comparative studies against existing state-of-the-art methods. This research is self-contained and accessible to users who may not always have extensive knowledge of cutting-edge research in machine learning, adversarial examples, and advanced statistical analysis. A comprehensive implementation of the introduced methods is made available online for public use. This includes a user-friendly Python package that integrates a flexible graphical user interface to facilitate easy operation. This research aims to inspire further exploration in the realm of reliable Bayesian estimation. In particular, we identify promising areas for future improvement and enhancement. In this study, we utilized the Robust Loss Hypothesis to investigate how altering a deep neural network's loss function impacts its performance. The Robust Loss Hypothesis suggests that broader loss functions produce more robust models. Our findings support this hypothesis, and we found that using a broader loss function than previously optimized leads to improved generalization performance. Additionally, we discovered that using a broader loss function during fine-tuning enhances the network's adaptability to diverse tasks. Our research also investigated whether using a broader loss function in a sequence of unsupervised pre-training and subsequent fine-tuning could aid in leveraging unlabeled data to improve supervised model performance. The results indicated that using a smoother loss function in pre-training is beneficial, but using an even broader loss function during fine-tuning actually harms generalization performance. Our study's findings provide new insights into the role of loss functions in deep neural networks and the underlying principles of their behavior. Moreover, these results open up potential new research areas in the context of robust loss hypotheses. The code used in this study can be found at https://github.com/jamestj/robloss. To accurately model the behavior of strongly correlated electrons in solids, ab initio approaches are developed to incorporate exciton condensation, a fundamental concept in quantum matter. Recent advancements in ab initio methodology have reached a pivotal stage for its application in solid-state physics. Our strategy, starting from generating reliable and electron-rich orbitals from first principles, enables the identification of excitonic signatures in band structures and their stabilization through the condensation of excitons. The application of our approach to 1T-TiSe2, a well-known excitonic material, confirms its validity and sheds light on the role of electron-phonon coupling in the process of exciton condensation. Computational results indicate that exciton condensation in 1T-TiSe2 is achieved when the chemical potential crosses the energy level of the lowest exciton, specifically at a electron density of approximately 6.25 x 10^-19 cm^2. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the electron-phonon coupling in 1T-TiSe2 plays a crucial role in the process of exciton condensation by modifying the energy levels of the bands and facilitating the softening of the highest vibrational mode, a condition not met under normal electron distribution. Our study offers a new understanding of the mechanism behind exciton condensation in 1T-TiSe2 and provides valuable insights into the role of electron-phonon coupling in quantum matter. Our ab initio approach is now poised to contribute significantly to the field of solid-state physics, enabling the accurate modeling of exciton condensation in a wide range of materials. Our methodology may also provide a useful framework for predicting and modeling new types of quantum matter. Finally, our study serves as a useful case study for those seeking to understand the application of ab initio methodology to strong-correlation systems, potentially offering a new approach for tackling long-standing challenges in solid-state physics. In the United States alone, dispatchers receive over 140 million calls each year, primarily from individuals who are anxious, panicked, or experiencing emotional distress. These individuals often form strong bonds with the dispatchers, who not only gather information but also serve as emotional confidants, counselors, and mediators between emergency services and callers. However, the substantial impact of dispatcher-caller interactions on the co-ordination of emergency services and their users is often underestimated. This research aims to uncover the hidden insights into dispatcher-caller relationships through automatic analysis of incident reports, revealing the complexities of social interactions within these relationships, and providing valuable insights that can improve the quality of emergency service provision. We employed a combination of textual data modelling, dimensional reduction, and clustering to explore the characteristics of incident reports, revealing subtle differences in language usage that reflect the emotional states of callers and dispatchers, as well as factors influencing interaction quality and incidence severity. These findings have the potential to be applied widely beyond emergency services. We also introduce R-RRCA, a novel approach for automatically summarising the underlying dynamics of social interactions between users and dispatchers through minimalised representations of incident reports, and demonstrate its effectiveness using a dataset of over 16K emergency incident reports. In our study, we synchronize the concepts of computability theory and optics to explore the idea of computational fun. We draw inspiration from Bishop's formulation of constructive reals as a probabilistic metric space, enabling us to extend this notion to real numbers with measures. We incorporate computability aspects by introducing the idea of a \emph{harmony} - a metric on the space of measures that ensures convergence of sequences. We then establish a connection between this harmonic topology and the logic of the material conditional, revealing that the space of measures becomes a complete topological space when equipped with the harmonic topology. We demonstrate that the harmonic topology has a natural representation as a probability space, allowing us to study the computability theory of this probability space and its interactions with other notions of computability theory, including but not limited to, the interplay between \emph{Roth} and \emph{Schanuel} sets within additive combinatorics. We conclude by drawing parallels between the suspended movement in the dynamics of computational fun and the shifting focus of attention in quantum mechanics. In a complementary thread, we explore the concept of computability theory as a form of musical composition, examining how the interplay between the analyst and the analyst's computer can be viewed as a choreographed dance between different instruments. We consider the elements of this musical composition, examining the roles of \emph{proof} and \emph{computational aid} as they relate to the elusive Schanuel set in additive combinatorics, a quest that resembles the search for a singular entity - the absolute music. We eventually arrive at a harmonious understanding of the analysis of computational models as a topological composition, and suggest that the topological space of measures provides a suitable framework for the composition of computability theory. We then reflect on how the theory of computability theory can be seen as a harmonious reflection of the underlying structure of numbers, drawing inspiration from the philosophical ideas of Bishop and Cutland. Finally, we conclude by observing that the theory of computability theory is a a a a a a a a a a a harmonious theory. We then revisit Bishop's probabilistic metric space, this time viewing it as a system in which the analysis of computational models is grounded, and in which the topological space of measures plays a pivotal role in the harmonious composition of computability theory. Our novel approach focuses on rewarding mobile game players with relevant in-game content by leveraging our advanced human-in-the-loop algorithm. This algorithm consists of three interconnected components: visually supported ranking of player behavior and item categories, selective sampling to accurately represent player preferences, and a supervised learning method to predict item ratings based on ranked examples. By combining these resources, we've developed a versatile solution capable of supporting a wide range of languages and can easily accommodate changes in the game environment without requiring extensive rewriting. Furthermore, the algorithm is designed for smooth operation at scale, making it suitable for large player bases. As evidence of its effectiveness, our algorithm achieved an impressive 85% accuracy in predicting human ratings after processing a relatively small dataset of 188 examples, and also demonstrated a 25% improvement in accuracy over a baseline model after training on our optimized sample set. Additionally, we've successfully deployed the algorithm in the game 'Episode: Complete Collection', where it's been used by over 15,000 players and has contributed to significant boosts in player engagement metrics and overall quality of the recommendations provided. Detailed evaluation results, including a comprehensive video case study, are available on our website. Furthermore, the algorithm is now openly accessible via GitHub, where it's being continuously maintained and supported by our team. We're excited about the potential for the algorithm to benefit other mobile game recommendation systems due to its notable achievements compared to state-of-the-art models, including a substantial edge over a top performing model that had been under development for two years. Specifically, our approach outperformed it by 10-20% in several key metrics, including accuracy and engagement ratings. One feature that sets our algorithm apart from other models is its reliance on player-created examples rather than explicit ratings, making it particularly suitable for games featuring a diverse range of items and scenarios. We're also exploring adaptations of the algorithm to support explicit rating-based learning and fine-grained recommendation tasks. It's worth noting that the success of our approach relies on the design principles of the game 'Episode: Complete Collection', which is characterized by its extensive collection of items and a range of hidden items that can be discovered by players. We believe that these factors contribute to the effectiveness of our algorithm and are committed to continuously collecting and analyzing player feedback to inform our recommendations. As a result, we're able to provide each player with a personalized view of the game world and relevant recommendations based on their behavior and preferences. Precision predictions in particle physics are crucial, and by 2024, experimental uncertainties in tau lepton properties will be a major limitation to theory. In the absence of experimental data, predictions relying on numerical techniques may be insufficient, and here we discuss how different approaches to describing the underlying physics can affect these predictions, with a focus on the structure of the proton. While certain predictions may be made using approximate models, in this talk we highlight cases where more detailed descriptions are needed to convey the true uncertainty in our predictions. We examine specific examples of tau decay, and also general tumor decay to illustrate our point. Furthermore, we consider how different numerical methods, such as lattice QCD versus QCD on and off the grid, can influence these predictions and which ones may be more suitable in the future. Ultimately, we wish to enable researchers to make accurate estimates of particle physics quantities with a level of uncertainty that is data-driven and guided by theory. With various approaches to describing the underlying physics, and differing opinions on numerical accuracy, we strive to create a unified strategy to achieve this goal. To this end, we propose a standardized evaluation of different techniques to compute proton structure and analyze the relative strengths and weaknesses of different approaches, and how they compare to the actual uncertainty in our predictions. By comparing and contrasting these different strategies, we aim to ultimately combine and align them, resulting in a collective understanding of the underlying physics and a clear vision for the future calculation of proton structure. In this way, we can ensure that our theoretical predictions for particle physics are indeed precision predictions. To that end, we outline a plan for a collaborative calculation that might involve experts in lattice QCD, and in the alternative theory of quark model description of hadronic matrix elements, and propose that it be led by the Worldwide Lattice Action Network (Lattice HDQCD Working Group). The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995, initially identified through spectroscopy, sparked controversy over its composition that persisted for nearly two decades.  We resolved this controversy by applying the APOLLO retrieval code to the available spectroscopy, ruling out any possibility of GJ 229B being a giant planet or object consisting of equal masses of hydrogen and helium, instead finding that GJ 229B likely consists of primarily hydrogen and carbon, with a small amount of oxygen, with a metallicity roughly one-third that of the Sun.  This composition is consistent with the formation of GJ 229B through the coreless nebular-accretion model.  Furthermore, our results suggest that GJ 229B's atmosphere is humid, with ammonia clouds covering its upper atmosphere, which red shifts the spectral light and results in the distinctive 1.6 $\mu$m absorption feature characteristic of ammonia. To effectively deploy predictive modeling and analytics to manage an urban epidemic, accurate estimates of individual movements and exposures are necessary. When testing a agent-based model of disease transmission on a urban system, it outperformed a corresponding average-contact model by a significant margin. Nonetheless, there are situations in which the average-contact model can provide reliable approximations of the agent-based model. Specifically, when focusing on a broad geographical area and a short-time horizon, both the agent-based and average-contact models yielded similar predictive errors. Interestingly, when time was factored in, the average-contact model often yielded greater errors than the agent-based model, particularly when considering departures and arrivals. Ultimately, when testing the complexity of both models using statistical and sensitivity testing, the average-model emerged as a viable option worthy of further exploration. Interestingly, the complexity of both models showed signs of stabilization as the urban system was analyzed. The implications of these findings are two-fold: firstly, the average-contact model can be a valuable tool for researchers and policymakers when limited resources are available; secondly, both the agent-based and average-contact models may be suitable candidates for testing in other mobility domains. Existing auction protocols often fall short due to their inability to handle multiple trading requests, low trading volume, and the potential for malicious actors to manipulate the system through altered trade history. To address these issues, we present a new protocol that ensures the integrity of trading data and allows for the exchange of private and public values in a secure and transparent manner. This protocol leverages a unique combination of techniques, including provenance, cut-and-choose, and zero-knowledge proofs to provide confidence in the trading process. Furthermore, our protocol enables trading entities to remain confidential while participating in auctions. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our protocol through a practical implementation of a financial market application. This application allows for the creation of digital tokens by matching the desires of entities to purchase and sell various assets. Through our analysis, we observe that our protocol achieves a good balance of fairness, high trading volume, and minimal trading complexity. Specifically, our results show that the probability of unfair gains for malicious actors is extremely low, amounting to $2^{-56}$, while the ratio of successful to unsuccessful trading attempts is approximately $2.89$, indicating a substantial increase in successful trading volume. Additionally, our results reveal that the size of encrypted token values ranges from $10^4$ to $10^6$ satoshis, which equates to a usable range of $1$ to $\approx 214$ euros, indicating the efficiency of our approach. This work represents the first development of a double auction protocol that uses blockchain and achieves a high level of security and efficiency in financial markets. Ultimately, our findings provide a new standard for developing secure and efficient trading protocols in various applications. This includes a user-friendly interface for participating in auctions via a web application, as well as educational materials for integrating our auction protocol into existing blockchain platforms. Additionally, we have launched a functioning auction testbed on the IPFS network to enable flexible and efficient auction participation. In recent years, researchers have placed significant emphasis on enhancing the Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD), a powerful feature extraction technique. Our work builds upon the 2020 research of Li et al., extending the scope of Kernel DMD (KDMD) to include uncertain systems via kernel regression. This novel approach, Kernel Education for Resolvent Partial Least Squares (KE-RPALS), aims to educate kernels in order to optimize various parameters in the reduced-order model. Our research demonstrates KE-RPALS to be a more efficient method when applied to problems with high levels of nonlinearity and uncertainty, when seeking to minimize the errors associated with reduced-order modeling. Furthermore, our kernel optimization technique is adaptable to a range of model reduction methods, including linear and nonlinear dynamics, as well as kernel-independent and structure-aware options. Ultimately, KE-RPALS is shown to effectively reduce the computational costs associated with modeling large datasets, specifically in cases involving partial differential equations and aerospace simulators. Specifically, efficient reduced-order models are achieved with an approximate reduction in computational time of two orders of magnitude. Additionally, our research reveals a direct relationship between the degree of nonlinearity present in a system and the number of iterations required by KE-RPALS to converge, with this number found to be less than ten instances. Lastly, our reduced-order models based on KE-RPALS are demonstrated to be resilient to variations in system parameters, with the reduction in computational cost also observed in cases where partial information of a system is available. Ultimately, KE-RPALS is shown to effectively bridge the gap between partial and complete kernel education, leading to efficient reduced-order models in both scenarios. Specifically, our research reveals that ke-RPALS can achieve an approximate reduction in computational time of two orders of magnitude when employed with partial or complete kernel education. Additionally, our results have been validated through various tests, including partial and complete information scenarios, as well as systems with and without nonlinearity, respectively. These experiments further illustrate the efficiency and robustness of ke-RPALS. We propose MemoNav, a robotic approach that chooses crucial memories for visual navigation by learning memory retrieval patterns from human-generated datasets.  By incorporating insights from recalled experiences, MemoNav enhances robotic navigation while also providing interpretable memory representations that resemble human-generated maps.  Experiments demonstrate MemoNav's ability to excel in challenging indoor navigation tasks with minimal robotic prior knowledge and limited training, achieving up to a 30% decrease in navigation mistakes when compared to experiences from mere random exploration.  Additionally, MemoNav's insights successfully transferred to a variety of unstructured scenarios in real-world settings, including searching for navigation prompts and selecting memorable locations for visual recognition.  With its ability to learn and replicate complex memory retrieval patterns, MemoNav offers a versatile approach for discovering relevant experiences and facilitating a wide range of tasks across various fields.  The proposed method is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/learnables/MemoNav.  Key features of the associated dataset, called MemoNav-100k, can also be accessed at https://differential-privacy.org/memonav.  This dataset features 100,000 instances of insightful memories, along with their associated retrieval patterns and is designed for use in various research areas, such as AI, robotics, and data science.  The dataset employs differential privacy mechanisms to ensure the protection of its subjects' information while also facilitating generalizable insights that are applicable in research and practical scenarios.  Specifically, differential privacy in MemoNav-100k prevents the detection of anonymous individuals by leveraging the release of artificially degraded data with the help of DP-KNN on human-generated maps.  This protection method not only discovers and erases sensitive information but also provides a range of degradation parameters, or budgets, that researchers can use to find the optimal balance between memory retrieval and protection from recognition. These observations led to the development of MemoNav, an approach that chooses crucial memories and facilitates a more efficient and accurate robotic navigation by learning to replicate the observed memory retrieval patterns and their relationships in human-generated datasets. By analyzing the measured spectrum, the research team derived a limit on the Hoyle state's branching ratio into the two-body final state relative to its radiative decay, amounting to 3.1 x 10^-5. The essence of this advancement lies in the recognition that fracture propagation is influenced by specific physical properties of the material. In this work, we introduce a phase-space analysis that distinguishes between two fundamental types of fracture instability - an oscillatory divergence and a tip-dividing phenomenon. By incorporating a material-dependent scale, we derive an analytical expression for the instability criterion, and find that the system exhibits a singular transition when this scale becomes zero. Numerical computations that consider a specific energy function reveal a branching regime associated with the oscillatory instability, while an examination of the kernel of a key integral phase-space equation shows that the tip-dividing instability can be seen as an abrupt change in solution behavior. Together, these findings provide new insights into the mechanism of both instabilities and highlight the importance of considering the inherent length and time scales associated with fracture propagation. Furthermore, we propose that the phase-space analysis can be extended to study instability in 3D fracture, and that this approach may also be applicable to other types of dissipative systems. Finally, we conjecture that the limiting scale associated with the branching and tip-dividing instabilities will converge to a universal value, and that this can be interpreted as a form of scale invariance. This may provide a significant breakthrough in understanding the underlying physics of fracture instability. Overall, we believe that the present study offers a fresh perspective on the computation of fracture instability, and that the proposed approach can be effectively used to generate universal results that are independent of any particular material properties or computational methods employed. Additionally, we hope that our work will inspire further research in this field to explore the underlying physics of fracture instability. This leads to the concept of k-solubility, defining a graph where the minimum number of observers needed to determine the distance between any two vertices is k. In particular, a graph that is infinitely soluble is known as infinite or  infinity-soluble. This research specifically focuses on finite graphs and specific infinite graphs, aiming to establish a linear relationship between the traditional metric dimension and the k-solubility parameter. Our approach incorporates density changes caused by salinity, temperature, and solute concentrations resulting from chemical reactions. Drawing from the work of Kummetz et al. (2018) and Kummetz and Krummeck (2020), we build upon their mathematical framework and modify the governing equations for enhanced porosity and permeability development. We further modify these equations to account for cohesionless accretion, erosion rates influenced by the stress state, and anisotropic erosion directions. The SystemC framework is widely used but has a number of drawbacks in its traditional form, mainly that it does not support the simultaneous development of both the hardware and algorithmic components of a project. Traditional machine learning models and their decision-making processes are designed to produce clear outcomes. However, in various real-world applications such as medicine and law, decisions are often accompanied by ambiguous assumptions made about the world. When these assumptions are quantified - expressed as probabilities - and structured - represented as rules, decision-making becomes a complex task. The current methods for dealing with such uncertainties are either insufficient because they don't utilize the learned information or rely on simplified decisions. This study introduces a novel class of probabilistic tree models that can explicitly handle and reason about quantified uncertainties in assumptions made about the world. The model achieves this by representing the uncertainties as arguments and acquiring a structured decision-making process through a new learning objective. The proposed model has several benefits, including improved robustness to changes in assumptions, enhanced exploration of the world's uncertainty, and a more detailed understanding of the decision-making process, as evidenced by empirical results on simulated and real-world data. The generated decision-making processes can also be interpreted and used in other tasks without the need for labelling. The Indecision forest's approach to handling uncertain assumptions and reasoning about them is a significant contribution to addressing a major limitation in current machine learning models. The DTW distance is significantly faster to compute than other edit distances, but its practical use has been limited by its long calculation time for some pairings. To address this issue, a recent optimization technique, PrunedDTW, reduces the DTW distance computation by eliminating unnecessary points in the alignment. An improved version, Early Discarding PrunedDTW, is presented here, which eliminates unauthorised points in the alignment even before the first discard. An empirical study confirms that PrunedDTW and Early Discarding PrunedDTW achieve the same level of accuracy, but the former offers significant performance gains. Building on PrunedDTW, an enhanced strategy is proposed to accelerate similarity search queries by leveraging PrunedDTW to filter incompatible neighbors earlier in the alignment. Experimental results indicate that PrunedDTW-based filtering yields a substantial increase in query processing efficiency, particularly when combined with an optimal pruning strategy of the k-nearest neighbors search. Implementation details and experimental data are available on GitHub under the term "Other". Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are the most popular graph neural networks, but they have several limitations when modeling long-distance graph connections. The reasons behind this limitation, called over-blurring, are not yet fully understood. In this study, we establish over-blurring as a mathematical issue that results from the GCN's spectral filtering convolution, and we demonstrate that regularization techniques cannot overcome it. Instead, we propose an alternative, called edge direct assignment, that addresses the over-blurring issue by allowing nodes to retain information about their target nodes, even if these nodes are far away. The regularity of the model can be monitored using the eigenratio ratio (ERr), a new metric developed in this study. In our experiments, we found that edge direct assignment led to significant performance improvements over existing methods, and it provided clear and interpretable results on synthetic and real-world datasets. The code for this study is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jb190772/OverblurringGCN.

Theoretical models proposing the existence of shadow matter, composed of weakly interacting particles, suggest that this matter could be produced in association with a Z boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To investigate this possibility, a search was conducted using data collected between 2016 and 2018, which amounts to a total of 137 fb$^{-1}$ proton-proton interactions at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The Z boson was detected using the observation of charged leptons produced in its decay, while a pair of jets was used to identify potential signals of shadow matter. Across a range of mass spectra from the Z boson and pair of jets, including scenarios where the shadow matter pairs have masses of 15 to 60 GeV and 7 to 30 GeV respectively, this study set new limits on the cross-section for a particular theoretical model as a function of the kinetic mediator mass, which ranged from 1 to 20 TeV. Furthermore, this study obtained a lifetime limit of 100 picoseconds for a dark matter model involving a complex scalar kinase. Additionally, this study obtained model-independent limits on the fraction of matter in the universe. Finally, this study derived limits on the anomalous magnetic moments of a particle for various matter models. All of these limits were found to be more stringent than previously established ones. To verify the results of this study, the simulation of proton-proton interactions was conducted using the Pythia and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO programs. Additionally, this study found that the search for shadow matter in the Z boson decay channel had the highest sensitivity among a range of theoretical models proposing the existence of shadow matter. To verify the accuracy of this study, the simulation of proton-proton interactions was conducted using the Delphes program. Based on these results, this study found that the search for shadow matter in the Z boson decay channel could be further improved through variations in the selection criteria of charged leptons produced in its decay. To verify the reliability of this study, the simulation of proton-proton interactions was conducted using the MC16XRD_RRun2_2016G 2.2.2 generator. Additionally, this study found that the search for shadow matter in the Z boson decay channel could be further improved through the use of neural network algorithms. To verify the consistency of this study, the simulation of proton-proton interactions was conducted using the MC16XRD_RRun2_2017C 2.2.
