The production and application of high-intensity isolated attosecond pulses are significantly hampered due to the inability to reliably generate them in the laboratory environment.  The uncertainty principle, which dictates that the shorter the pulse, the broader the spectral range and the higher the pulse energy, poses a major challenge in achieving pulses that are both extremely short and have low energy.  To overcome this limitation, a new concept involving the coherent manipulation of multoelectron targets is introduced through the implementation of a pump-probe attosecond pulse generation scheme.  This method utilizes an initial drive laser pulse to create a preformed low-energy seed in a target within a few hundred attoseconds, which is then released by a second probe pulse that is delayed and much weaker.  By optimizing the strengths and durations of the pump and probe pulses, as well as the natural decay rate of the initial low-energy seed, it is possible to achieve pulses with durations of approximately 160 attoseconds, peak intensities of $10^{11}$ W/cm$^2$, and spectral ranges of 6.2 eV.  The introduced coherent pulse generation scheme has been shown to be capable of producing pulses with specifications that closely match those of pulses generated in the laboratory and natural fs laser pulses, significantly advancing the production of high-intensity isolated attosecond pulses.  The introduced pulse generation scheme has been shown to be robust to variations resulting from the interaction of pulses with the preformed low-energy seed, as well as to significant modifications in the strengths and durations of the pump and probe pulses.  The introduced pulse generation scheme has been shown to be efficient in producing pulses with specifications that closely match those of pulses generated in the laboratory and natural fs laser pulses, even in scenarios where the strengths and durations of the pump and probe pulses differ greatly from those that were initially optimized.  The stability of the introduced pulse generation scheme has been attributed to its reliance on a temporal partitioning mechanism in which the initial low-energy seed is rapidly released following the absorption of energy from the probe pulse.  The introduced pulse generation scheme has been shown to be capable of achieving pulse generation regimes that include both the single-ionization and double-ionization of multoelectron targets, as well as a novel two-step pulse generation regime in which the initial low-energy seed is first ionized and then rapidly released following the absorption of energy from the probe pulse.  The introduced pulse generation scheme has been shown to be stable and versatile, and can be employed to generate pulses with various characteristics, including negative charge, controllable polarization

We examine explosion solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, particularly in areas beyond a convex obstacle. Assuming a certain superlinear nonlinearity, we show that well-defined, bounded solutions with a finite $L^2$ norm can develop into explosive solutions as time progresses, given that the obstacle's potential function meets specific criteria and a certain threshold is exceeded. This tends to the expense of the solution's global $L^2$ norm, with its Hartree approximation approaching a standing wave convergence. Additionally, we address analogous issues related to the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, revealing distinct solution behaviors. This work follows from major advancements in nonlinear Schrödinger equation research, notably the recent proof of stable, bounded solutions' global existence and their eventual approaches to explosive solutions. Our findings also generalize and adapt earlier works by Feigo and Kapitanski to include those byerg, Feig, Kapitanski and Grossi in the presence of a potential function. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for solving partial differential equations. Despite their potential, they are hindered by a critical issue: the need for an extensive number of training points which is not feasible in many real-world applications. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed solutions but they have not entirely resolved the problem yet. In this study, we present a novel contribution by introducing an important factor that plays a role in adjusting the flow of information in physics-informed neural networks and propose an adaptive nodal creation technique based on this factor. This technique requires training the network with a relatively small number of nodes and allows the network to learn the details of the solution at a micro-scale while confirming its accuracy at a macro-scale. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique by applying it to simple examples. Furthermore, we explore its generalizability to more complex problems in dynamics and physics, analyzing its performance and confirming its efficiency. The growing freight sector plays a crucial role in economic development, yet its spread and use are heavily influenced by various factors including the geographical location, industry types, and environmental conditions. This study aims to advance the concept of dependency-fragility in the freight sector by creating a network of insights that can help understand how certain characteristics of freight operations spread across different areas. To do this, a methodological framework is developed and applied to Toronto and Montreal by collecting and analyzing data from service providers, freight users, and other stakeholders through semi-structured interviews and questionnaires. The analysis involves constructing a complex network of relationships and identifying key nodes, patterns, and trends to measure the fragility of freight systems in each study area. To evaluate the accuracy of the approach, the results are validated by comparing the predicted outcomes with actual feedback received from interviewees and industry experts. Furthermore, the findings reveal valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of freight systems in Toronto and Montreal, as well as general best practices that can guide the improvement of freight services and planning decisions. The study contributes to the existing literature by integrating and refining existing concepts into a unified theory of freight dependency-fragility, and it is expected that the developed approach will be beneficial in understanding and analyzing freight systems in other areas. The research has several limitations, and future studies are suggested to further validate the approach by increasing the sample size and scope, and by using statistical methods to build and test a theoretical framework that can explain the spread of freight practices. The proposed framework can aid freight scholars and practitioners in making informed decisions and strategies to improve the performance and planning of freight operations. To facilitate this, the full report of this research, including the data collection instruments, and the methodology used to analyze and interpret the results, are made available on the designated open-access platform. The study also utilizes open-access data sources and promotes collaborative research by making available the R code for reproducing the results and shared research data. The Freight Ecosystem Dependency-Fragility Insight Graph developed in this study can be accessed via a public online platform. The study also explores the concepts of freight visibility, density, and fragility in detail, and it is shown that the applied approach is equally effective in understanding these characteristics. The research demonstrates that the freight sector is a complex and dynamic system that is sensitive to geographical and environmental factors. The study reveals that the performance of freight services is closely linked to the quality of the infrastructure, the availability of technology, and the skills of the people involved. The data analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the freight ecosystem

Furthermore, we establish the importance of channel features in supplementing ocurrence features for tasks that require invariant response to orientation, as well as explore the potential of combining orientation convolutional architectures and channel features through residual learning. The success of Deep Learning methods in computer vision tasks has created a high demand for efficient and adaptable neural networks designed for point cloud processing. Due to the unique characteristics of their input, such as sparsity, variability, and regression challenges, current frameworks face substantial obstacles. This study addresses these issues by introducing a novel graph convolutional network, GCN2, which combines graphical and convolutional components. GCN2 employs an optimized graph construction method from dynamic graph networks to create a semi-implicit graph framework, thereby ensuring fast and seamless assembly of the graph within deep network training. The proposed graph construction method balances accuracy and computational efficiency by using a parameterized technique to determine the nearest neighbors for each node, thereby reducing computational complexity. The results of GCN2's performance in various point cloud processing tasks, such as semantic segmentation, oriented bounding box detection, and centered bounding box detection, demonstrate its superiority over alternative graph convolutional networks. The success of exoplanet hunting has led to the discovery of more than 4000 stars hosting planets, but the composition of the planets themselves remains largely unknown. By studying the chemical properties of their host stars, scientists can gain valuable insights into this mystery. 

Drawing from previous studies and the analysis of spectral data from the HARPS/N2 and XSHOCK programs, we've established a reliable method for determining the chemical composition of a cohort of 102 stars hosting terrestrial-type planets.

Our analysis focuses on the core properties of these stars and the composition of their planets, examining both the overall elemental composition and the relative abundances of key elements versus planet mass and radius. 

The results reveal both expected and unexpected patterns, with the core properties of these stars and their planetary companions closely linked through gravity and evolution. Notably, we've identified a few stars exhibiting enhanced or diminished levels of key elements compared to the overall sample, potentially shedding light on the unique formation environments of their planetary entourages.

These findings contribute to a growing understanding of the relationships between stars and their orbiting planets, paving the way for further research into the planetary mass range and the ultimate goals of this study: determining the composition of individual planets and the structure of planetary atmospheres and interiors.

Computer experiments can be efficient tools for analyzing complex systems that cannot be accurately modeled analytically, often producing a large amount of output data in the form of time series. In contrast to traditional methods, which typically treat each simulation run as a separate observation, this work proposes incorporating insights from medical imaging and quality control to develop an innovative approach for processing and interpreting this data. By evaluating the entire time series rather than focusing on a single metric, this method enables researchers to identify an unknown parameter affecting the system by leveraging the inherent structure of the data through the use of functional principal component analysis. Subsequently, this parameter can be estimated by minimizing a metric measuring the distance between simulated and real performance profiles, ultimately resulting in confidence intervals for the parameter of interest. The method's performance and effectiveness are demonstrated through case studies involving well-known models, such as the reliability-based smooth tolerance model and the lawson equation. A comprehensive simulation of these models' output further highlights the approach's ability to accurately estimate the parameter even when the method's assumptions are slightly violated. Additionally, this approach is versatile and can be adapted for estimating other system parameters as well as modeling differences between real and simulated data. Software for replicating the results is available through the R package named MCA. This research seeks to inspire further exploration in the field of computer experimentation through novel applications of time series analysis. Future studies may develop supplementary methods such as using spectral measures, incorporating measures of uncertainty, and exploring ways to choose an optimal sampling rate for collecting output data. Furthermore, this research may be extended to design experiments through the use of replication, response surface design, and other experimental design methods. Future studies could also involve leveraging data from other sources, such as sensor feedback and real-world data, to further enhance the validation of computer models. In particular, this research may be expanded by investigating ways to incorporate and make use of real data within simulation models, potentially through the development of bi-directional coupling methods and shared latent variable approaches. The latter could potentially involve adapting techniques from the shared latent variable literature to estimate costs and generate real data samples that better reflect the behavior of the system. This research could result in new metrics for evaluating model performance and providing guidance on running sufficient sample sizes in Monte Carlo studies. On a broader scope, this research may contribute to advancing the use of computer experiments in engineering design and the applied sciences through the design and analysis of experiments that incorporate both real and simulated data. Data-sharing issues and data-protection laws like GDPR and CCPA pose significant challenges to training resilient neural networks from diverse data sources. Even when allowed to collect and use neighbor datasets in the parameter space, the benefits for resilient networks are still largely unknown. In this work, we provide theoretical guarantees for the effectiveness of regional queries in enhancing the robustness of neural networks. Through experiments on various real-world datasets, we demonstrate that regional queries in conjunction with adversarial training can significantly improve the robustness of networks, especially in the high-confidence regime. Furthermore, regional queries induce little to no degradation in the model's original performance. The simplicity and effectiveness of our approach make it a viable option for addressing data-sharing restrictions and improving the robustness of neural networks. In addition, we found that regional queries can be integrated into existing training methods like MixUp and Virtual Adversarial Training without sacrificing the model's original performance. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com(avisingh11/Regional-Resilient-Neural-Networks.

It focuses on high-pT jets associated with isolated photons, which are less susceptible to modifications caused by the medium and collective effects within it. By comparing the fragmentation functions and the average number of sub-jets in jet-photons between Pb-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions, it was found that there are noticeable alterations to jet fragmentation in the central region of Pb-Pb collisions. However, these changes are less pronounced in the forward region. Most importantly, it was observed that the modifications to jet fragmentation in the central region are less than those found in inclusive jet measurements. Various factors are considered to explain the differences between these measurements, including collective effects and parton energy loss. Furthermore, it was found that there are enhancements to high-pT charged particles within jets in the central region, but not in the forward region, which is consistent with energy loss. Finally, using jet-photon pairs, it was possible to calculate the average distance that partons travel, which is in agreement with predictions from the YUKE parton energy loss model. Overall, these findings provide new insights into parton energy loss and collective effects in Pb-Pb collisions. They also highlight the potential for further investigating jet fragmentation using data from proton-proton and Pb-Pb collisions, as well as future electron-ion collider experiments. Recent research involving Apéry-type series has yielded hitherto unforeseen outcomes, such as an integral representation via colored multiple zeta values and an analogous series with odd-indexed terms. This current paper builds upon those findings by extending the analysis to series with both even and odd indexed terms, specifically those aligned with the second alternative convolution of beta and gamma functions. An alternate approach is provided via a direct recomputation of the Apéry-type series through colored multiple zeta values, with various examples demonstrated. Furthermore, a SHS (single horizontal slice) inversion formula is developed, enabling the expression of any colored multiple zeta value as a finite sum of two series, with terms alternating in parity. This invention leads to novel representations of several constants, including $\zeta(3)$, $\zeta(5)$, $\zeta(7)$, and $\zeta(9)$. Additionally, a chronology of research is presented, linking Apéry-type series to objects such as polylogarithms, polydifferentials, and motivic functions, as well as their numerical counterparts. Finally, some prospective roads to exploration are suggested. \end{abstract}

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for this object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that it possesses remarkable proper motion, corresponding to over 1200 years in the recent past, as evidenced by its large angular separation of 13.3 arcseconds. Additionally, its brightness has undergone substantial fluctuations over the past three years, while its WISE and ZTF photometry appear to be consistently representative of a ~5000K brown dwarf. Nevertheless, its spectral energy distribution, observed through Keck/MOSFIRE, can be accurately modeled by a photosphere characterized by temperatures of 3400K, nearly six times lower than its WISE-estimated temperature of 4600K. Its large proper motion suggests that it is likely not in an equatorial star formation zone but instead may be an unusually fast-moving sub-stellar object or extreme PMBD. Further analysis of its motion, using the Gaia DR3 data, indicates that it may be sharing a trajectory with nearby objects, including a ~7000K white dwarf, whose provenance is unclear but could be linked to the unusual properties of WISEA J153429.75-104303.3. This association raises the possibility that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 could be a novel type of astrometric double star, featuring the aforementioned object, along with the aforementioned white dwarf. It is also conceivable that during its rapid motion, the Gaia DR3 may have captured a rare image of a binary system, with WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 acting as a "mishap" that has enabled researchers to identify unusual celestial entities whose existence would have gone undetected through observations of this object in a single state. In light of these new findings, the most plausible hypothesis is that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 is an extreme parasitic brown dwarf with a temperature of ~3400K and a mass of ~0.021~M. This type of object is expected to be extremely rare, with a mass ratio of 0.6 to 0.9, and would likely have a much longer and more irregular motion, deviating from the expected smooth trajectory, as it is thought to be an outlier in the equatorial plane of a nearby star

Based on the DGLAP evolution equation, we develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to compute parton distribution functions at different energy scales by utilizing low-order parton distribution functions. Our method enhances existing approximations by incorporating higher-order terms related to the DGLAP evolution equation, resulting in predictions that match QCD predictions at leading order. We evaluate the accuracy of our parton distribution functions at leading order, comparing them to QCD predictions using MRST2006 parton distribution functions as a reference. Our results demonstrate that incorporating higher-order terms improves parton distribution functions, especially for gluons, and we contend that this improvement arises from better alignment with the DGLAP sum rule. We also found that our parton distribution functions meet the DGLAP stability criterion, indicating smooth evolution towards higher energy scales. To test the validity of our parton distribution functions at leading order, we performed fits to inclusive electron data, revealing agreement within 10% between our predictions and experimental data. Our parton distribution functions are the first to satisfy the DGLAP stability criterion and represent an efficient, leading-order approximation to QCD parton distribution functions. They can be utilized at low energy scales (2-3 GeV) where existing parton distribution functions are not well-constrained, enabling improved description of inclusive data at those energies. To facilitate the use of our parton distribution functions in xBDM fit to inclusive hadron data, we implemented them in the NNPDF3.0 framework. Our research indicates that parton distribution functions at leading order can be an effective tool for improving the understanding of QCD at low energy scales. They can be used in conjunction with existing parton distribution functions to enhance our understanding of QCD and test its principles at high energy scales. To that end, we also suggested a strategy for combining the advantages of low and high energy parton distribution functions, potentially leading to more accurate results. Our work opens the door for further research on parton distribution functions at leading order, and we believe that they can contribute new insights to the field of QCD. By comparing observed and modeled data for a set of 222 star-forming galaxies, we examine the reliability of star formation rate estimates derived from SED fitting using various models. These models include observed galaxy templates, flexible physical models, and models specifically designed to study active galaxy nuclei. We find that even the most sophisticated physical models struggle to accurately represent the diversity of galaxy spectral energy distributions, leading to inaccurate star formation rate predictions. On the other hand, template-based models yield more plausible results, and the choice of galaxy template set is found to be a primary factor influencing the resulting star formation rate predictions. Furthermore, we find that even when using these template-based models, spurious predictions of extreme star formation rates can occur when there are signs of a active galaxy nucleus or other spectral energy distribution features indicating extreme star formation. However, such signs can often be identified through simple tests, and in cases where they are present, the resulting distributions of star formation rate predictions for individual galaxies become heavily biased. Ultimately, we conclude that while SED fitting has utility for other purposes, it is not a reliable method for accurately estimating global star formation rates. Rather, we recommend relying on bracketing a particular emission line and using template-based models or physical models specifically designed to study active galaxy nuclei to obtain more plausible results. Additionally, we find that these linear SED fitting methods can be used to effectively remove contaminated data and improve the reliability of emission line-based star formation rate estimates. With this approach, we are able to obtain emission line-based star formation rates that are comparable to those obtained through more complex modeling methods. Specifically, we apply this technique to the database of 222 galaxies, using the bracket-$\gamma$ line and a set of galaxy template sets developed from observed galaxies, to obtain emission line-based star formation rates that are consistent with those predicted by more complex physical models. This work presents an innovative approach to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions by integrating data from various devices that capture user input.
Each input method - keyboard, touch screen, pen - is treated as a distinct language, which is then combined to form a unified mathematical language (ML).
A primary challenge lies in aligning inputs from different sources and languages, which is addressed through the development of a novel framework incorporating language model-based alignment and sensor-driven encoding techniques.
Furthermore, the paper introduces a pioneering ML language model to facilitate generative language modeling for the integrated ML language. 
Our method is demonstrated through an example application, where sensor-driven input data is used to recognize mathematical expressions in a unified format.
Our system's effectiveness is evaluated in terms of its ability to learn the integrated ML language, determine expression boundaries, and assess its generative quality using a range of metrics. 
While challenges with ML language modeling are identified, the proposed approach offers a groundbreaking solution to recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions from diverse user inputs. 
Our experiment results demonstrate an average 77.91% accuracy in expression recognition and a median F1-score of 0.7856 in boundary detection. 
Our approach provides a pioneering solution to leveraging various user inputs and their respective languages to recognize mathematical expressions.

This study presents an innovative approach to synthetic speech generation utilizing non-statistical methods. A syl-la-ble-frequency-pattern-language, referred to as MedLang, was developed to generate speech through the application of median values representing various syl-la-ble lengths, word frequencies, and content. A conversation between two individuals was created within MedLang to facilitate learning, and the model was challenged with spoken sentences as input to mimic spoken human dialogue. Our results demonstrate that MedLang outperforms existing synthetic speech models, and we formally introduce the concept of spokenness to measure speech quality. Additionally, our findings underscore the significance of controlling syl-la-ble frequencies in speech synthesis. Furthermore, we conclude that non-statistical approaches can effectively generate spoken language, and we envision numerous possibilities for extending our method to other language generation tasks. A demonstration of our model is available at https://youtu.be/jN8z4M5M5GQ. Code for MedLang, including the model and training data, can be accessed at https://github.com/vivek_yadav/MedLang.

To capture patterns in time sequences of Type Ia Supernovae spectra, we introduce a stochastic autoencoder designed for sequential data. This model, RRNet, uses a novel latent space reconstruction framework, and we demonstrate through cross-validation that it outperforms existing methods in generating accurate redshift estimates and signal-to-noise ratios for simulated spectra. Furthermore, we identify the intrinsic variability in spectral sequences through the divergence of multiple realizations in the latent space, and reveal how this source of noise affects our model's performance. Our analysis also explores the potential of RRNet to contribute to cosmology by generating mock spectra with diverse redshift evolution. Our approach does not rely on pre-training with generic neural network architectures, instead leveraging the sequence structure of the data to determine the network's parameters. This innovative model contributes to the development of more efficient methods for analyzing spectral time sequences, and its efficacy has implications for future research in generating synthetic spectra with diverse redshift evolution. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming geometrical relationships between individuals may provide a more accurate representation of the spread, akin to modeling infections within spatially organized environments. Hypergraphs capture these connections by encapsulating higher-order interactions within the inherent structure of the graphed relationships. Our research explores the transmission of epidemics within hypergraphs, examining the critical thresholds at which the disease spreads through the network. Through an inversion of the spectral graph operator, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the extinction of the epidemic, and subsequently, the asymptotic critical threshold as the hypergraph doubles in connectivity. Additionally, we apply this method to investigate the epidemic dynamics within two specific hypergraphs: hypercubes and complete k-partite hypergraphs. In the case of the cube, we show that a simplified approximation of the spectral limit, derived from the generalized Lubotzky-Weisfelter theorem, is asymptotically equivalent to the exact critical threshold as the dimensionality of the cube increases. For the complete k-partite hypergraph, we demonstrate that the spectral limit achieves an exact match with the asymptotic critical threshold, and further, that this value represents a generalized universality for all hypergraphs with equally distributed vertex degrees. The methodology employed in this research is expected to contribute to future investigations in the field. As a result, research has emerged to employ formal techniques in managing multithreaded  software's verifications.  This paper introduces McMini, a innovative model checking  tool designed to verify multithreaded applications' correctness, that employs DPOR  and incorporates three key adjustable elements: thread-activation policies,  shared-data management strategies, and work-till-abandonment, all of which can  be customized to optimize the tool's performance.  Through a thorough evaluation of 15 open-source, multithreaded applications, McMini demonstrates its ability to detect  errors in models faster than other state-of-the-art model checking tools.  Additionally,  our research reveals that adjusting McMini's parameters can even improve its detecting  performance after initial training.  This research offers two primary contributions:  first, we introduce McMini, a flexible model checking tool for verifying multithreaded  programs that accommodates a variety of parametric strategies, second, we provide  empirical evidence showing that adjusting these parameters can lead to improved  detection performance.  This research sets the stage for future work on optimizing  McMini's parameters to maximize its potential in model checking multithreaded  software. Among these filters, Bloom filters and Cuckoo filters are the most widely used, however they have significant drawbacks: Bloom filters frequently return false positives and Cuckoo filters often expand significantly to maintain an acceptable false positive rate. Both issues become more severe as the size of the database grows. In contrast, existing solutions such as Cuckoo Hashing Vectors and HyperBloom filters offer better performance but with limited applicability: they can only guarantee a low expansion rate or low false positives, not both at the same time. This study introduces a new filter called Xor Filter, which offers a trade-off between these two performance metrics. Unlike existing filters which insert modulated hash values, Xor Filter utilizes unmodulated hash values when inserting elements or querying for membership. This study also presents various optimization techniques for reducing memory usage and computational overhead, based on properties of hash functions. Experimental results demonstrate that Xor Filter outperforms both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in terms of speed, compactness and overall efficiency. Moreover, this study provides evidence that a single hash function is sufficient for small to medium-sized databases while two hash functions are more effective for larger databases. The theory unfolds through the application of spectral sequences, and we utilize this framework to investigate the homotopy cofiber of a spectral map. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the spectra of a group's and its finite subgroups, demonstrating that their profinite spectrum is a "homotopy lim^1" limit with regards to these subgroups. We also explore the equivariant homotopy type of general linear spectra and develop computations for specific 2-groups, such as the dichromatic spectra of SL(2,R) and its absolute grade spectrum. Lastly, we outline approaches to addressing open questions, one of which involves identifying the minimal model of a group's homotopy action spectrum. The other question concerns whether the homotopy action spectrum is equivalent to a rational spectrum when the group's rational radius is contractible. The latter inquiry is significant because it is anticipated that the answer will be negative, and this expectation is grounded in preliminary findings. Conversely, it is hypothesized that the rational radius will be contractible for 2-rigidity groups. We have verified this conjecture for all 2-rigid profinite groups with a prime number of generators. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the de facto standard for image classification tasks. However, they place a significant computational burden on resource constraints. The usual approach to mitigating this is neural network pruning, which can save hardware costs but complicates backpropagation during the training process. Current methods either preserve the original model's accuracy but incur excessive computation due to redundant operations or disregard the model's structure, resulting in decreased accuracy. We introduce ClickTrain, a pioneering approach that uses fine-detailed architecture-preserving pruning and dynamic computation scaling to meet the resource limitations of image classification CNNs during the training process. We leverage the sparsity of the information in the CNN weights to refine the pruning process and the computational requirements, allowing for the efficient training of resource-constrained hardware while maintaining the original model's accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves state-of-the-art results on the ImageNet dataset, outperforming the baseline model in terms of both accuracy and computational cost. Additionally, we show that ClickTrain can successfully train very deep CNNs on the ImageNet dataset, a feat that cannot be accomplished through common pruning and training techniques due to the model's significant computational requirements. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/hjkwon/ClickTrain. We hope this work will contribute to the development of next-generation neural network training methods that can effectively employ the principles of neural network pruning and dynamic computation scaling to meet the resource constraints of resource-constrained hardware. ClickTrain, in particular, can serve as a training method, allowing the efficient training of CNNs that can achieve the same level of performance as their full-model counterparts but with a significantly reduced computational cost. Our work is centered around the concept that neural network pruning and deep CNNs are not mutually exclusive, despite what has been previously suggested in the literature. We achieve this by integrating the principles of the DPC and EFN methods, which we then combine with new pruning and dynamic computation scaling strategies, all while maintaining the original model's accuracy. We introduce a primary-dual method to solve Restricted Markov Decision Processes, which involves breaking down the original Markov Decision Process into simpler 'primary' processes and using dual variables to model 'dual' processes. By taking the average of these processed policies, we achieve a key approximation property. Building on this approach, we develop an iterative algorithm based on Lagrangian programming principles. We evaluate the performance of this algorithm through numerical tests and find it to be competitive with the best known existing methods. Notably, we observe that our approach has a natural application in the Stochastic Shortest Path problem. We propose an alternative primal algorithm for RMDPs that relies on a Markov State-Action Value Function, which we believe holds significant theoretical value. We evaluate the efficiency of this algorithm through numerical tests and find it to be comparable to the best known existing methods. One notable aspect of this algorithm is its applicability in solving multiple existing Markov Decision Processes, including those associated with games and paths. We conclude by highlighting potential areas of improvement in our current approach. Specifically, we observe that our methods may not be suitable for solving discrete RMDPs where states can transition directly to themselves. We speculate that dual variables may not effectively capture the complexities involved in such situations. We point to existing research that suggests probabilistic graphical models may provide valuable insights in addressing this challenge. Certain sheaf cohomology rings can be generated from a complex of finitely graded vector bundles. We examine an algebraic model that represents this cohomology and utilize it to analyze supersymmetric quantum mechanics coupled with multiple fermions. By doing so, we generate a free bosonic action that encodes both topological and dynamical information from the original fermionic quantum mechanics. Further, we explore connections between our model and Leray's residue mechanism to compute cohomology, achieving this via both direct computation and indirect calculation through homotopy Morse functions. In a theoretical study, we focus on a dynamic treatment framework where treatment and observation decisions are made sequentially. We investigate a scenario in which an agent is part of an online learning process and, using historical data, predicts the likely future rewards associated with various actions. We find that, even in the absence of positive correlation among outcomes and with past actions, pessimism is inevitable in this scenario, thereby compromising coverage. To mitigate this limitation, we develop a Bayesian learning strategy that incorporates uncertainty into reward predictions, enabling the agent to balance exploration and optimization. Specifically, the Bayesian approach ensures that expected reward predictions remain pessimistic, thereby guaranteeing that long-term coverage is not compromised. We demonstrate that our approach can be implemented through simple, efficient algorithms and illustrate their performance using empirical examples in new and established models. We also establish a formal connection between our strategy and the long-term coverage objective, providing theoretical guarantees for the generated policies. To our knowledge, this work presents the first theoretical analysis of pessimism in online learning frameworks and the first strategy to address it through Bayesian adaptation. Furthermore, our empirical studies reveal that the proposed approaches significantly outperform existing strategies. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. We're revving up the figure-eight track with the motor puzzle puzzle, a reversible racing game where drivers navigate a 64-unit grid. The game's score keeps growing as drivers collapse their race track, merging adjacent squares. Their total distance traveled is represented by a tally of all individual moves. This motor puzzle puzzle metric is akin to a symmetric number $\mathfrak{N}_n$ that counts all possible collusions of $n$ square arrays. At the lower end of this expansion, a pattern of cycle multipliers emerges for both scores, thereby facilitating their calculation. This work delves into the motor puzzle puzzle metric, along with associated symmetry sequences, examining both of their numerical underpinnings. To obtain detailed information from CT scans, x-rays interact with various materials in the body. However, CT systems emit x-rays of different energies, and the resulting measurements are affected by signal attenuation and noise. As a result, image reconstruction involves more complex processes than traditional single-energy scans. Our study introduces a novel distance minimization approach for recovering tissue composition, taking into account multiple energy levels and interactions, as well as independent noise effects. The proposed framework relies on prior knowledge about the materials to formulate a non-convex variational problem, and relies on iterative algorithms to obtain stable solutions. Our experiments involve numerical simulations and comparison with existing reconstruction methods. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/pkowalski4/Polyenergetic-Reconstruction.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and language-specific dictionaries. To overcome these obstacles, we concentrate on developing methods for single-shot data generation and dictionary learning. From a given handwritten page, our approach produces a collection of single-word sentences by assuming them to be compositional, meaning they consist of sequences of constituent parts such as prefixes, domains, suffixes, and letters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on the datasets "NLP-UA Text" and "AMT-Hilltop", which showcase notable performance enhancements compared to existing techniques. Notably, our results reveal a significant boost of up to 14 Character Error Rates with only 25% fewer annotations. We also introduce a new dataset, "NLP-UA Text", specifically designed to facilitate the development of compositional HTR models. Additionally, we provide a detailed evaluation of the "AMT-Hilltop" dataset, which consists of 13,610 pages of handwritten text collected through crowdsourcing. We further present a new word-sentence decomposition model based on Hidden Markov Models, making our code available at https://github.com/darthvader611/HTR_Composition. We successfully achieved training and testing on real-world data without any prior knowledge of the language, achieving a 12 Character Error Rates on the "NLP-UA Text" dataset. On the "AMT-Hilltop" dataset, we achieved an error rate of 19.5. This level of performance surpassed existing methods by an error rate margin of 5.91. We also demonstrated that through pre-training on synthetic data generated using our approach, we could achieve a 10 error rate margin on real-world data. To analyze the structure of heavy nuclei, researchers combine different models to integrate unique aspects. For example, in the region of superheavy nuclei and for nuclei with a high neutron-to-proton ratio, calculations often focus on the behavior of valence particles outside a more stable core. To accurately predict properties like energy, deformation, and alpha decay, researchers use a novel computational method that merges the ab initio Lanczos equation method with a stratified approximation for the core. This approach, projectized as the ab initio computational method for heavy nuclei (ABCHe), enables researchers to incorporate high-energy valence particles and semi-interactive interactions. Notably, the ABCHe method produces predictions in the form of energy eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, allowing researchers to make more informed choices about potential energy surfaces. We apply the new method to study the ground state of the nucleus $^{264}Db$ and demonstrate its effectiveness in modeling heavy nuclei. We also compare the new method with more traditional approaches, such as the generator coordinate hypothesis, finding similar results. The merged method has several advantages, including improved accuracy and a simpler theoretical foundation. The approach, however, does not easily generalize to nuclei with strong correlations in their cores. The predictions from the ABCHe method are consistent with experimental data and provide a valuable reference point for future studies. Furthermore, the method enables researchers to establish a clear connection between structure and decay properties, highlighting the importance of understanding the detailed distribution of wave functions in decay processes. We expect the ABCHe method to contribute significantly to the ongoing research into superheavy and proton-rich nuclei, enabling precise calculations of their properties and a deeper understanding of their behavior. The merged method will likely be an essential tool in future research into stable and unstable nuclei across the entire table of elements. The calculations have been fully documented and are available for public access through the arXiv repository. The code used in these calculations, projectized as the ABCHe method, is an iterative improvement of the IT-SFB code, which is based on the TNS code originally developed by T. Duguet. The final IT-SFB code has been successfully used in a range of applications, including the study of deformation in low-dimensional quantum valence systems and the modeling of high-energy particle behavior in heavy nuclei. In various topological systems, certain band structures serve as indicators of protected modes that appear at certain points, typically denoted as zero-energy modes. These systems can be categorized into different types, such as topological insulators and superconductors, based on specific characteristics. To gain a deeper understanding of these categories, we investigate whether the protected modes in these systems share common attributes. To this end, we establish a set of concepts, including mode location, superposition, localization, and degeneracy, and examine them across different types of topological insulators and superconductors within the context of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. We find that the protected modes in these systems exhibit specific characteristics, such as pair-wise degeneracy and localized modes, and demonstrate that these concepts are transferable to other systems through effective representation. Additionally, we illustrate the application of these concepts in distinguishing between different topological categories through the example of a superconducting loop. Our study provides a framework for further exploration of these concepts in other topological systems. We also propose a method for characterizing topological insulators through the generation of sound waves. We show that the established concepts are compatible with both finite and infinite system sizes and provide examples to demonstrate our findings. Our research has the potential to contribute to the development of new technologies based on topological insulators if the protected modes can be successfully transferred to the bulk. To achieve this, we examine various coupling schemes between the boundary and the bulk. We find that in the case of a three-site chain, we can successfully transfer the mode to the bulk if a specific characteristic is implemented, thus achieving a topological band structure with multiple bands. Our research has the potential to expand our understanding of the properties of topological insulators. We also propose an alternative method for characterizing topological insulators through the generation of sound waves. These waves can be generated by exciting the electrons in the system, and we find that in the case of a non-superconducting SSH model, we can distinguish between different topological categories through the generated sound waves. These categories include topological insulators and superconductors, and we demonstrate that the resulting sound waves exhibit specific characteristics, such as pair-wise degeneracy and localized modes, thus matching the characteristics we found in the superconducting SSH model. Our study provides a new perspective on the classification of topological systems through the generation of sound waves. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly benefits from using CUDA, which has evolved over the years to support various low-level memory management functions. Effective memory management in CUDA is crucial for achieving optimal performance in both host-based and device-based programs. This study addresses the lack of efficient memory management in GPU object-based programming by introducing a novel memory manager, DynaSOAr. This research provides an in-depth analysis of the memory management challenges in object-based programming on GPUs, and offers a new perspective on the internal structure of objects to enhance memory access for the CUDA runtime environment. Additionally, DynaSOAr is designed to be a generic, reusable module that can be easily integrated into existing object-oriented frameworks, and is accompanied by comprehensive performance benchmarks that demonstrate its efficiency and adaptability on a range of systems. Furthermore, we explore the possibilities of concurrent programming on GPUs by applying DynaSOAr to a real-world application, specifically by converting a sequential algorithm to a parallel version that outperforms the original in terms of speed and memory usage. Our findings show that DynaSOAr achieves significant performance improvements of up to 30% in various benchmarks, and also accurately predicts memory usage with an average error margin of 2.4%, further solidifying its potential as a reliable memory manager for object-based programming on GPUs. This research offers an innovative memory management approach that could serve as a foundation for the development of efficient, scalable concurrent memory management systems on GPUs. As a proof-of-concept, DynaSOAr outperforms the current state-of-the-art memory manager by precision, and significantly improving the efficiency of object-based programming on GPUs by a factor of up to 30%. Furthermore, we have successfully applied DynaSOAr to two real-world algorithms, specifically by converting a sequential algorithm to a parallel version that achieves better performance and reduced memory usage, and also demonstrated the efficiency of DynaSOAr in various numerical library functions on GPUs. Our study has also compared DynaSOAr with other leading memory managers on GPUs, and found that it outperforms them in almost all benchmarks by precision, and significantly improving the efficiency of object-based programming on GPUs by a factor of up to 30%. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach to provide certain guarantees for Bayesian Networks, a type of probabilistic machine learning model. By integrating concepts from reliability theory, probabilistic inference, and constraint programming, we derive a method to ease constraints on probabilistic circuit variables and establish a bounded influence on the reliability of corresponding circuit outputs. This method enables the generation of secure regions for reliability quantification in Bayesian Networks, akin to Lipschitz stability in metric learning. Our approach is demonstrated through the analysis of a secure driver-vehicle system and an examination of implications for driver behaviour. This method has potential applications in various domains where model accuracy and reliability are essential. In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) displaying both zero-viscous flow and phonon modes, we define a measure of mechanical stiffness associated with the latter. We demonstrate that both modes are impacted by the presence of a common potential modulating the BEC's density. However, the effect of the potential on the stiffness of phonon modes differs significantly from its influence on the characteristic frequency of zero-viscous flow modes. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we investigate how the mechanical stiffness of phonon modes is affected by changes in the density of the BEC and its underlying potential. Our analysis yields a measurable value for the stiffness in a dual-species BEC displaying a supersolid and dipolar liquid coexistence. Furthermore, we find that while the characteristic frequency of zero-viscous flow modes can be influenced by the magnetic field in a controlled manner, the mechanical stiffness of phonon modes is largely insensible to similar variations in the magnetic field. Our research does, however, present a limitation - the application of our analytical methods to supersolid spin polarized BECs reveals that they are unable to display both zero-viscous flow and phonon modes within the same parameter space. Our study also extends to supersolid ferromagnetic spinor BECs where we investigate the relationship between the mechanical stiffness of phonon modes and the magnetic stiffness of the condensate. This versatile design utilizes a resistance to measure temperature, and achieves precision of 0.24{\deg}C due to its 12-bit resolution. A quick review of the sensor's properties reveals support for on-die clock generation, multiple gain factors, and a self-adjusting bias current feature. Furthermore, the sensor's design is adaptable to custom IC projects and has been fully characterized in a 0.5$\mu$m CMOS process. Last but not least, the sensor's design integrates two power-efficient analog circuits, including a fully balancing fully differential amplifier and a fully integrating charge-redetection voltage converter, each with their own unique error-reducing characteristics. We introduce a novel technique, the Distorted Resolvent method, to construct Nash equilibria in various game-theoretic applications. This method leverages the properties of the Nash equilibrium-like solution concept, the Distorted Resolvent, which outperforms traditional perturbation techniques. By utilizing the Distorted Resolvent, we develop local and global analysis tools that can be applied to a broad range of situations, including infinite and finite games, as long as they meet specific criteria. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate the efficiency of the Distorted Resolvent method in constructing accurate Nash equilibrium approximations. Furthermore, we show that this method can be efficiently implemented when the games it originates from have a particular structure. We anticipate that the Distorted Resolvent method will serve as a vital tool in contemporary game theory and dynamical systems. Additionally, we believe that it will contribute to the development of novel approaches in both fields. In brain tissue, the regulation of substance distribution is essential, with excessive accumulation indicating abnormal conditions, such as brain disorders or drug overdoses, that can lead to cell damage. Furthermore, we explore the potential of our model in predicting factors contributing to acute brain disorders caused by substance overdose. With its versatile structure, our model can be applied to various brain disorders, providing a general framework for understanding substance regulation and addressing potential shortages or imbalances in brain tissues. Modern single-image deblurring methods rely heavily on clear image datasets for training, 
which creates a discrepancy between blurred images and real-world deblurred images.
To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes a pseudoblur 
generator to incorporate knowledge from motion-blurred images.
By cross-training on paired blurry-nonblurry image pairs, the pseudoblur generator 
learns to generate realistic blur patterns, including those caused by human and scene 
movement, which are often difficult to simulate synthetically.
This unique feature enables our approach to better tackle a broader range of blur 
patterns, particularly those resulting from non-stationary objects.
Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method, 
especially when dealing with deblurring long-lasting motion and mixed blur patterns. 
Although computationally efficient, our method also achieves state-of-the-art performance 
when evaluation metrics such as PSNR and SSIM are used to measure accuracy. 
Furthermore, qualitative analysis confirms the ability of our approach to remove 
artifacts and achieve sharp, natural-looking images.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex data. Unlike traditional CNNs, which utilize vector-matrix multiplication for convolution, GCNNs employ matrix-matrix multiplication with the help of graph filters. However, the graph filter used in GCNNs lacks a clear theoretical foundation, differing significantly in both function and theoretical sense from classical signal processing filters. This discrepancy in theory hinders our understanding of the graph filter's purpose, making it difficult to develop and effectively use graph filters. To address this, we suggest a new method for matching GCNN filters to traditional signal processing filters, providing a theoretical link between GCNN and signal processing. This matched filtering method not only resolves the ambiguity in graph filters' definition, but it also provides a necessary and sufficient condition for effective information transmission through the graph network. Additionally, this method allows us to establish the minimal requirement for successful graph convolutional neural networks. A step-by-step illustration using a simple example is provided to help readers comprehend the technical aspects. Experimental results on synthetic data also demonstrate the method's effectiveness in predicting network parameters. Finally, we explore the relation between the proposed matched filtering method and popular GCNN structures, revealing insights that can improve their performance. By considering labor as a measure of persistence in motion, we explore how it affects the collective behavior of AOUPs and investigate the conditions under which they exhibit sub-Diffusion, non-Diffusion, and Ballistic-like behavior. Our findings also reveal a transition from weakly coupled to strongly coupled dynamics in the limit of low labor, and we connect this change to changes in their collision frequency and efficiency. Understanding these dynamics may provide insights into the design of artificial swarms for a variety of applications. Ultimately, we demonstrate that by tuning the labor of AOUPs, it is possible to achieve a wide range of search strategies, from enhanced local exploration to widespread coverage. Additionally, we identify potential applications and leave behind promising paths for future research. Interestingly, the analyzed dynamics exhibit similarities with the behavior of their passive counterparts when considering their relative velocity and dispersion. However, the primary difference lies in the underlying driving mechanisms, as well as the resulting dynamics and their underlying physics. This research presents HUMBI, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 41,110 full-body pose data captured from various viewpoints. Leveraging our collection, we introduce an innovative competition focused on enhancing the visual realism and plausibility of computer-generated characters through animation methods. We propose three challenges to drive research in this area, with detailed problem definitions and evaluation criteria. Typically, this involves using a multilingual model to capture task representations in each language. However, there's a lack of understanding about what these task representations consist of and how they can be effectively captured. In this research, we use neural network architecture designs to investigate the components of task representations and develop methods to weakly guide cross-lingual model transfer. Our results show that by incorporating domain-specific representations into a multilingual model, NLP models can be successfully transferred from English to low-resource languages, achieving performance levels comparable to models trained from scratch with unlabeled text data. Importantly, our research indicates that task representations are composed of both general task features and domain-specific characteristics. Additionally, our findings suggest that the effectiveness of cross-lingual model transfer is heavily influenced by the characteristics of the target language dataset. Our code is available online at https://github.com/jadelimtl/NeuralTaskDepictions. This work was inspired by questions raised in a previous study [2]. A simple yet effective approach to video super-resolution, BasicVSR++, has been developed with improved propagation and alignment methods that outperform the current state-of-the-art method, BasicVSR, in a comprehensive evaluation. In addition, BasicVSR++ has achieved superior performance on VR quality evaluation metrics, resulting in a more efficient and scalable architecture with reduced parameters and a faster inference speed. Achieving this success involved refining the propagation and alignment procedures in Video SR with residual channel attention, leading to the development of Enhanced Propagation and Alignment (EPA). A major contribution of BasicVSR++ is the introduction of Alternative Forward and Backward (AFB) forward passes to enhance the propagation process and reduce parameters, all while maintaining comparable accuracy to previous methods. Furthermore, BasicVSR++ has successfully integrated scalable filters in Video SR with RCNN to further enhance the propagation process without increasing parameters. Additionally, BasicVSR++ has improved the alignment process in Video SR with residual channel attention by introducing the low-cost cross-correlation (CLC) alignment scheme to reduce parameters and inference time. Consequently, BasicVSR++ has achieved the current state-of-the-art performance in video super-resolution with a parameter count of 0.54 M and an inference speed of 13.6 fps. A thorough evaluation of BasicVSR++ has been carried out on various video enhancement tasks and datasets, demonstrating its superiority and leading to its adoption in several video enhancement tasks. Specifically, BasicVSR++ has achieved VR quality scores of 42.73, 42.45, and 42.29 on VidLoUper+ benchmark videos at resolutions of 256, 256, and 256, respectively, representing a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art method. A detailed analysis of the evaluation results is also provided to explain the performance of BasicVSR++ and identify its areas for improvement. Therefore, BasicVSR++ has been designed as a simple, efficient, and accurate video super-resolution method with broad applications in video enhancement tasks. The code for BasicVSR++ has been made available on the popular open-source platform GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Ingram-Liu/BasicVSR++.pdf. Specifically, BasicVSR++ has been carried out on the widely used deep learning frameworks PyTorch and MMDetection at the following links: https://github.com/Ingram-Liu/BasicVSR++/tree/master/pysr and https://github.com/Ingram-Liu/BasicVSR++

In complex real-world environments with limited computing power, it's impractical to create massive training datasets. Instead, we can utilize theoretical models to generate simulated data. However, designing training systems that utilize theoretical models is challenging due to their inherent complexity and the need to balance simulation accuracy with scalability. In this research, we explore the application of modular training methods in model-driven reinforcement learning, focusing on multi-task training where the environment is partially observable and dynamic. We show that using theoretical models in multi-task reinforcement learning is feasible and can lead to significant performance improvements over standard deep reinforcement learning methods. Furthermore, we identify potential pitfalls in multi-task training and propose a modular training system that avoids these issues, achieves similar performance as state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning methods, and significantly reduces computational costs. Recent advances in recommender systems have led to the success of collaborative filtering (CF), especially its improved versions, in guiding real-world consumer behavior. However, the traditional CF methods face significant challenges in handling the emerging characteristics of sparse, subjective, and group-based user preferences. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel CF approach called UBCF, which leverages an unsupervised user-clustering technique to group users with similar preference patterns. The novel aspect of UBCF lies in its ability to model each user's preferences as a combination of three interconnected aspects: user-clustering structure, item selections, and preference strength. The effectiveness of UBCF is demonstrated through extensive experiments conducted on multiple real-world datasets, which show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art CF methods while maintaining reasonable computational efficiency. Furthermore, the results of our practical evaluations confirm that UBCF's predicted recommendations are subjective to individual users and exhibit high coherence compared to existing CF methods. To validate the reliability of UBCF, we also developed a series of robustness tests, which demonstrate the reliability of UBCF's predicted recommendations across different parameter settings. The proposed approach showcases a significant improvement in prediction accuracy, with an average boost of 6.2% over the best performing baseline CF methods on six real-world datasets, while maintaining a reasonable prediction time of only 86.5 ms per update. The proposed User-Centric Bicluster-based CF approach provides an innovative solution to addressing the emerging characteristics of sparse, subjective, and group-based user preferences in modern recommender systems. The code for UBCF is available on GitHub at the indicated URL. Additionally, the predicted user-clustering structure of UBCF is shared on GitHub under the name "UCbf_clustering_structure". Specifically, the results of our experiments have shown that UBCF can be effectively utilized to enhance the sparse preference prediction, subjective preference aggregation, and group-based relevance ranking tasks in sparse preference datasets. The presence of magnetic activity has a significant impact on the formation of absorption features in a star's light, which can mimic the effects of stellar activity on a planet's transmission signal observed in radial velocity data. To better understand and isolate the signs of planetary activity, we investigated how magnetic activity influences absorption patterns in solar data from the HARPS-N solar telescope. We analyzed numerous activity indicators and identified several new markers of magnetic activity that can serve as indicators in solar data, which can also be applied to exoplanet hunting efforts to identify elusive small planets. We found that these activity indicators can reliably detect magnetic activity even at low levels of activity, and are less susceptible to the limitations of current observation capabilities. Additionally, we found that these activity indicators can be used in conjunction with existing indicators to improve our detection and identification of small planets. Notably, we discovered that the most effective way to detect a particular type of magnetic activity, referred to as "magnetic features," was through the use of narrow-band observations, which yielded a detection rate of 85%. We further examined the characteristics of "magnetic features" and how they can provide valuable insights into the physical conditions of the sun's chromosphere, which can also be applied to the study of other active stars. Our study paves the way for the incorporation of these activity indicators into the analysis of radial velocity data, which can aid in the identification and characterization of small exoplanets and improve our understanding of the sun's behavior and its implications for other active stars. A robot's ability to navigate through its environment depends on its capacity 
to make informed decisions by assessing situations that emerge during navigation 
as a sequence of reasons and conclusions. This work, drawing from the logical 
concept of deduction, introduces an innovative and autonomous navigation system 
known as the Profound Active Deduction System (PADS). By incorporating reasons 
related to the robot's objectives, surroundings, and movements, PADS generates a 
conclusive sequence of locations for the robot to visit in order to achieve its 
goals and collect relevant environmental information. The systematic structure 
of PADS's reasoning enables the detection of dead ends and promotes the 
discovery of multiple solution paths to a navigation problem. Additionally, 
PDAS's focused and directed exploration characteristics facilitate seamless 
extension to more complex scenarios involving objectives and reasons that may 
be hard to cover using more traditional methods, such as randomized or greedy 
approaches. The theoretics behind PADS has been formally established and 
demonstrated in an independent proof of its fundamental properties. The system 
has been successfully tested and validated through a series of simulation 
experiments, showing its capabilities to navigate through challenging scenarios 
involving multiple objectives, reasons, and potential obstacles. The results 
obtained from these experiments, along with the integration of public tools such 
as OpenCV and A* algorithm, make the system even more efficient and effective, 
as evidenced by its high performance in the navigation evaluations. A 
documentation of the system, along with its related tools, is available online 
at https://pads-system.org. This research has been inspired by the ideas 
presented in the book "Reasoned Action and Decision for Autonomous Piloted 
Vehicle" and has drawn from the Profound Active Deduction (PAD) model for its 
conceptual foundation. Additionally, it has been influenced by the related 
work in deduction, decision theory, and robotic navigation. The associated

A quantum approximate optimization algorithm variant, called Variational Hybrid Quantum Classical Algorithms, has been proposed to solve combinatorial optimization problems. Further development has led to VHQC's hybrid Bayesian version, which we apply to optimize the well-known MaxCut problem on a complete graph. The new method integrates a quantum circuit with a classical Bayesian booster, yielding impressive results. Specifically, our experimental findings show that the Bayesian version outperforms its classical and quantum counterparts by a significant margin when the problem size increases. Moreover, we discovered that the Bayesian up-to-date method can achieve accuracy at least one order of magnitude better than its counterparts. particular, our experiments indicate that the Bayesian version is approximately three orders of magnitude more efficient than its quantum counterpart when the problem size increases. This outstanding performance stems from the Bayesian booster's capacity to learn the problem's structure, which translates to a substantial advantage in running experiments on NISQ devices. Additionally, we found that the Bayesian version's resilience to noise far exceeds that of its quantum counterpart. Specifically, our experiments indicate that the Bayesian version's performance degradation due to noise is about 10 times less than that of its quantum counterpart. This exceptional robustness is attributed to the Bayesian booster's ability to integrate diverse measurements, thereby making it more resilient to noise. In summary, our experiments indicate that the variational hybrid quantum classical algorithms' performance can be significantly enhanced through the integration of a Bayesian booster. particular, the new hybrid algorithms achieve substantial improvements in accuracy and robustness, which is likely to be invaluable in solving real-world optimization problems. This paper introduces an innovative method to identify areas where two ellipses intersect. Our approach avoids intricate calculations commonly associated with this problem. Instead, we utilize a straightforward geometric technique that relies on basic arithmetic to determine intersection regions. The method's simplicity makes it suitable for teaching and modeling purposes in computer science. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a tangible example, solving a long-standing inquiry regarding the intersection of two specific ellipses. The solution employs our proposed method to pinpoint the areas where these ellipses intersect. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted to calculate the volumes of shapes formed by merging these ellipses through the cut-slice method. Specifically, we demonstrate how to accurately calculate the volume of a solid formed by taking a segment of one ellipse and slicing it with another ellipse. This adaptation not only enhances the simplicity of our initial method but also makes it more versatile, yielding a general technique that can be applied to a broad range of scenarios. The areas where the ellipses intersect, as well as the volume of the resulting solid, are illustrated through graphical visualizations that provide a tangible representation of our solution. The concept of q-training is initially explored within a dynamic framework. 
The traditional objective of q-learning, which seeks to maximize long-term rewards, 
is redefined as a goal in a time-varying environment where rewards change over time.
Our research identifies several challenges in dealing with evolving environments.
To address these issues, we introduce the notion of synchronizing the temporal context with the decision-making process.
As a result, our study splits the environment into separate instances, each represented by a state-action state (SA)-tuple, 
which we refer to as a situation.
Situations are organized into a graph where the transition from one situation to another unfolds over time.
The concept of situation relevance is also introduced to describe situations that are closely related to the current one.
Based on these findings, our research outlines a series of theoretical steps to develop a q-training algorithm for situations.
Finally, a potential application of our research is presented through an example scenario relating to situation relevance in a dynamic environment context. 
The example illustrates how situations connected through the sharing of relevant information can evolve over time.

Furthermore, this model's integration with AAC and ACE enables end-to-end vertebrae localization and identification in CT scans. Evaluation based on public datasets and extensive experimental comparisons confirm the superiority of this integrated solution over competing models. This paper explores the properties of relative quantum homology in the context of symplectic geometry. We define and investigate the relative quantum homology of a pair $(X,\phi)$, where $X$ is a symplectic manifold and $\phi$ is a rational transformation, which can be seen as an extension of the existing concepts. We also identify the first and second cohomology groups of this relative quantum homology and derive a mirror theorem for pairs under specific conditions. Furthermore, we extend the existing results on Einstein equations from the mathematical field of symplectic geometry to the realm of relative quantum homology. Additionally, we leverage $\mathbb{D}$-modules to analyze the properties of relative quantum homology, which leads to the introduction of new concepts and ideas. We also demonstrate that the properties of $\mathbb{D}$-modules can provide valuable insights into the properties of relative quantum homology. Lastly, the paper ends with a discussion on future research directions in this field. These research directions include further investigating $\mathbb{D}$-modules, applying mirror symmetry to study phase space, and exploring the connections between relative quantum homology and linear logic. The exoplanet K2-22 b, orbiting a G-type star at a close distance, undergoes the most frequent among the transient brightness variations known as Stuart billows. Analysis of LBT data reveals that these billows are likely caused by the movement of clouds consisting of tiny dust grains. This conclusion is drawn from the observations' high resolution and the similar patterns observed in multiple phases. The estimated speed of the clouds is 5,000 to 20,000 km/h. The abundance of these dust grains in the atmosphere suggests that they must form close to the star's surface and before reaching the equilibrium temperature, where they would immediately decompose. This process implies that the atmosphere of K2-22 b is experiencing significant changes, possibly triggered by the movement of molten metal fluids. The available models do not fully explain the observed characteristics of the billows and thus a more complex scenario is indicated. The observed dust grains may be the result of an uneven distribution of the star's energy on the atmosphere, causing the outer layers to expand and contract at different speeds. This dynamic could also be responsible for the desiccation of the atmosphere, leading to the exposure of the dust grains. The exposed dust grains then accumulate on the ground, where they are eventually consumed by a gas flow that is more frequent and intense than previously estimated, happening around every 36.5 hours. This strong wind is likely responsible for eroding the atmosphere and could be among the strongest in the known exoplanets, with a speed of at least 4.5 km/s. The consumption of the dust grains by the wind supports the theory that the root cause of the billows is a complicated internal process, possibly involving the movement of chemical components in the atmosphere. This complex scenario is further confirmed by the analysis of the phase shift in the LBT data, which does not match the expectations for a cloud traveling through the atmosphere. Instead, the data suggests that the phase shift is not uniform, indicating that the clouds are not moving independently, but are instead being affected by hidden factors. The observed variations in the billows also vary depending on the perspective, both in terms of amplitude and shape, which is likely to be caused by the uneven distribution of the dust grains across the atmosphere. To achieve this, I identify and examine the conflict between mathematicians and philosophers at the University of Cambridge during this era. Despite initial obstacles, mathematicians were eventually able to establish their credibility as contributors to natural philosophy, ultimately paving the way for the development of modern scientific methods. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates considering both the kinetic effects and the electrostatic forces encountered in plasma.  To investigate magnetic island formations during reconnection, researchers utilize advanced simulations integrating magnetohydrodynamics with the particle-in-cell model, enabling them to study the reconnection process in an increasingly more accurate framework.  By incorporating an adaptive algorithm to integrate the kinetic effects of plasma into the magnetohydrodynamic simulation, researchers evaluate the impact of various integration techniques on magnetic island merging.  Simulation results show that incorporating kinetic effects via adaptive PIC significantly differs from the conventional magnetohydrodynamic model, particularly in the reconnection rate, electric potential, and 3D vortex structure, with the integrated model exhibiting a substantially higher reconnection rate close to the kinetic estimate.  Furthermore, the integrated model demonstrates that the electric potential at the reconnection site is nonlinear, contrasting with the prediction of the magnetohydrodynamic model.  Additionally, the integrated model reveals distinctive, electron-scale current concentrations in the reconnection neighborhood.  Lastly, the integrated model demonstrates that the reconnection rate is sensitive to the PIC integration volume, a finding that has important implications for the development of more accurate turbulence-transport models in magnetic reconnection. This chapter's main objective is to provide an overview of the Coder project, 
whose main version was introduced in the 1993 paper titled "A Man-Machine Interface for Coding Natural Language Sentences Based on Word Embeddings". 
Significant advancements have been made since then, leading to the development of the Coder2 version, 
which is the foundation for the Amanuensis system presented in this chapter. 
Coder2's updates include the incorporation of several advanced technologies. 
The Amanuensis system aims to assist experienced coders in training new recruits 
by demonstrating their coding practices in an understandable manner. 
In this system, an analysis module assesses a coder's performance and identifies areas 
where the new coder could benefit from the established coder's expertise, 
following which the Amanuensis system generates an explanatory text. 
A substantial part of the system involves building a knowledge base that outlines 
the coding principles and guidelines as well as their integration, 
which is based on the Coder2 framework. 
This chapter also includes an evaluation of the Amanuensis system's performance 
using human and machine evaluation methods. 
Additionally, we have made available the Amanuensis system's code and knowledge base for 
research purposes on our website at http://nlp.ksu.edu.ewc. 
In the following sections, we begin with an overview of related work in systems 
that promote best coding practices, followed by a detailed explanation of the Coder2 framework, 
after which we present the Amanuensis system design and its functional components. 
We conclude with an evaluation of the system, followed by future work and research directions. 
By promoting experienced coders as role models, the Amanuensis system aims to 
enhance its reputation and promote its coding standards within its organization. 
To achieve this, the system demonstrates an analysis of an new task 
and explains its approach in an easy-to-understand manner, while also providing 
valuable insights on how to integrate it into the new task at hand. 
We hope that the system will be useful to coders within our organization who 
wish to enhance their knowledge and promote our coding standards.
